items.title: Left, right and two-sided ideals
Ideal criteria and intersections of ideals
The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals
In a commutative ring, $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum r_i s_i$, and $(a)=Ra$
The sum $I+J$ and product $IJ$ of two-sided ideals
The sum and product of two-sided ideals are two-sided ideals
The kernel of a ring homomorphism is a two-sided ideal
The quotient ring $R/I$ with $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$
Multiplication of additive cosets is well defined if and only if the additive subgroup is a two-sided ideal
For a two-sided ideal $I$, the additive cosets form a ring $R/I$ with identity $1+I$
The canonical projection $R\to R/I$ is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $I$
For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the congruence-class ring $\mathbb Z/n$ is the quotient ring $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$
A ring homomorphism whose kernel contains $I$ factors uniquely through $R/I$
First isomorphism theorem for rings: $R/\ker f\cong\operatorname{im}f$
If $S$ is a subring and $I$ is an ideal of $R$, then $S+I$ is a subring, $I$ is an ideal of $S+I$, and $S\cap I$ is an ideal of $S$
Second isomorphism theorem for rings: $S/(S\cap I)\cong(S+I)/I$
If $I\subseteq J$ are ideals of $R$, then $J/I$ is an ideal of $R/I$
Third isomorphism theorem for rings: $(R/I)/(J/I)\cong R/J$
Correspondence theorem: ideals of $R/I$ correspond to ideals of $R$ containing $I$
Prime ideals and maximal ideals in a commutative ring
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal
$R/M$ is a field if and only if $M$ is a maximal ideal
Every maximal ideal of a commutative ring is prime
In a nonzero commutative ring, every proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal

The zero ideal of $\mathbb Z$ is prime but not maximal
$2\mathbb Z$ is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$ but is not a subring under the library's unital convention
$R\times\{0\}$ is the kernel of $R\times S\to S$, so $(R\times S)/(R\times\{0\})\cong S$

pages.title: Euclidean Domains, PIDs and UFDs: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The integers are a Euclidean domain with Euclidean function $\delta(b)=|b|$

pages.title: Polynomial Rings, the Division Algorithm and Roots

items.title: The polynomial ring over a commutative ring as finitely supported coefficient sequences with convolution
items.strategy: For a commutative ring R, define R[x] as the set of functions a:N->R with finite support, write a as a formal sum, define addition coefficientwise and multiplication by finite convolution, and identify R with the constant polynomials while defining x as the sequence supported at 1.

items.title: Coefficientwise sums and convolution products of finitely supported sequences are finitely supported
items.strategy: Choose bounds beyond the supports of the two coefficient sequences. Addition vanishes beyond their maximum, while every summand in a convolution coefficient beyond the sum of the bounds contains a zero factor.

items.title: Polynomial convolution makes R[x] a commutative ring containing R as its constant subring
items.strategy: Verify the additive laws coefficientwise. For multiplication, use finite-sum reindexing to prove associativity, commutativity and distributivity, identify the sequence supported at 0 with value 1 as the identity, and verify that the constant-polynomial map is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

items.title: Degree, leading coefficient and monic polynomial, with the zero polynomial having no degree
items.strategy: For a nonzero finitely supported coefficient sequence, use the maximum of its nonempty support as the degree and its value there as the leading coefficient; call it monic when that value is 1. State explicitly that the zero polynomial has neither a degree nor a leading coefficient.

items.title: Finitely supported coefficient sequences and trimmed finite coefficient lists define the same formal polynomials
items.strategy: Send a nonzero finitely supported sequence to the unique list ending at its degree and send the zero sequence to the distinguished zero polynomial; pad a finite list by zeros in the reverse direction. Prove the maps are inverse and preserve addition, convolution, degree and leading coefficient.

items.title: Degree inequalities for sums and products over a commutative ring
items.strategy: For nonzero polynomials, inspect coefficients above the relevant support bounds. Prove deg(f+g)<=max(deg f,deg g) when f+g is nonzero, identify the coefficient of degree deg f+deg g in fg as the product of leading coefficients, and conclude deg(fg)<=deg f+deg g whenever fg is nonzero.

items.title: Over an integral domain, degrees add under multiplication of nonzero polynomials
items.strategy: The top convolution coefficient is the product of the two nonzero leading coefficients; the domain hypothesis makes it nonzero, while every higher coefficient vanishes by the support bounds.

items.title: A polynomial ring over an integral domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Use the product-degree theorem to show that a product of two nonzero polynomials cannot vanish, and inherit commutativity and the distinct zero and identity through the constant-polynomial embedding.

items.title: The units of R[x] over an integral domain are exactly the constant polynomials whose values are units of R
items.strategy: If fg=1, degree additivity forces both factors to have degree 0; compare constant coefficients. Conversely, the constant polynomial attached to a unit has the constant inverse.

items.title: Evaluation and roots of a polynomial in a commutative target ring
items.strategy: Given a unital ring homomorphism phi:R->S between commutative rings and s in S, define f(s) as the finite sum of phi(a_i)s^i. A root is an s for which this value is 0; distinguish the formal polynomial from the element obtained by evaluation.

items.title: Universal property of R[x]: a coefficient homomorphism and the image of x determine a unique ring homomorphism
items.strategy: Show directly that evaluation preserves addition, identity and convolution multiplication, and verify that the formula agrees with evaluation of the corresponding trimmed coefficient list. Any homomorphism extending phi and sending x to s must send each finite sum of monomials to the evaluation formula, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates by iteration
items.strategy: Define R[x_1,...,x_n] recursively by R[x_1,...,x_0]=R and adjoining one polynomial indeterminate at a time. Record the canonical coefficient inclusions and that the iteration makes all named indeterminates commute.

items.title: A polynomial ring in finitely many indeterminates over an integral domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Induct on the number of indeterminates, using the one-variable domain-inheritance result at the successor step and treating the zero-variable ring as R.

items.title: Division by a monic polynomial over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Induct on the degree of the dividend. If its degree is below the monic divisor, stop; otherwise subtract the leading coefficient times the appropriate power of x times the divisor to lower the degree. Prove existence and uniqueness over every commutative coefficient ring; for uniqueness, monicity keeps the top coefficient of the divisor times a nonzero quotient difference nonzero even when the ring has zero divisors.

items.title: Factor theorem over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Divide f by the monic polynomial x-a. The remainder is constant, and evaluating the division identity at a identifies that constant with f(a), giving f(a)=0 iff x-a divides f.

items.title: Division algorithm for polynomials over a field
items.strategy: Normalize a nonzero divisor g by its invertible leading coefficient to a monic polynomial, apply monic division, and absorb the scalar into the quotient. Degree additivity over the field proves uniqueness, including zero dividend and constant divisor cases.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a Euclidean domain with degree as Euclidean function
items.strategy: Combine the domain theorem with the division algorithm and take the degree of each nonzero polynomial as its natural-valued Euclidean function; the remainder is zero or has smaller degree.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a principal ideal domain
items.strategy: Apply the published theorem that every Euclidean domain is a PID to the preceding Euclidean structure.

items.title: The monic greatest common divisor of two polynomials over a field
items.strategy: For f and g not both zero, define gcd(f,g) as the unique monic generator of the principal ideal (f,g). Relate this ideal definition to the divisibility characterization and explicitly leave gcd(0,0) undefined.

items.title: Bézout identity and the Euclidean algorithm for polynomials over a field
items.strategy: Run repeated division until the last nonzero remainder, back-substitute to express it as Af+Bg, and normalize it to be monic. Prove that it divides f and g and that every common divisor divides it, agreeing with the ideal-defined gcd.

items.title: Every irreducible polynomial over a field is prime
items.strategy: If irreducible p divides fg and does not divide f, then gcd(p,f)=1. Bézout gives Ap+Bf=1; multiply by g and use p|fg to obtain p|g.

items.title: Every nonzero nonunit polynomial over a field factors into irreducible polynomials
items.strategy: Use strong induction on degree. An irreducible polynomial is the base alternative; a reducible polynomial is a product of two nonunits of strictly smaller positive degree, to which the induction hypothesis applies.

items.title: For every field F, F[x] is a unique factorisation domain
items.strategy: Existence is the preceding induction lemma. For uniqueness, use that every irreducible is prime to divide one factor on the other side, cancel associates in the domain, and induct on the number of irreducible factors, including units and constants.

items.title: For a nonconstant p in F[x], the ideal (p) is maximal and F[x]/(p) is a field exactly when p is irreducible
items.strategy: If p is irreducible, every polynomial not divisible by p has gcd 1 with p, so Bézout gives an inverse for its residue class. Conversely, a nontrivial factorization produces nonzero nonunits or zero divisors in the quotient. Reconcile the conclusion with the published maximal-ideal/field-quotient equivalence.

items.title: A nonzero polynomial of degree n over an integral domain has at most n distinct roots
items.strategy: Induct on degree. If there is a root a, factor f=(x-a)q; every other root b satisfies (b-a)q(b)=0, and the domain plus b!=a forces q(b)=0. The zero-degree case has no roots.

items.title: Every finite subgroup of the unit group of an integral domain is cyclic
items.strategy: Let G be a finite subgroup of the unit group of a domain D. Commutativity makes G a finite abelian group; handle the trivial group directly. For nontrivial G, let 1<n_1|...|n_r be its invariant factors and put e=exp(G)=n_r. Every g in G is a root of the nonzero degree-e polynomial T^e-1, so the root bound gives |G|<=e. The invariant-factor formulas give e=n_r<=n_1...n_r=|G|; equality forces r=1, and the one-invariant-factor criterion makes G cyclic.

items.title: Over an infinite integral domain, equal polynomial functions come from equal polynomials
items.strategy: If f and g agree at every element, then f-g has infinitely many roots. The root bound forces f-g to be the zero polynomial.

items.title: A polynomial of degree two or three over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in the field
items.strategy: A root gives a linear factor by the factor theorem. Conversely, a nontrivial factorization of total degree two or three has a degree-one factor; normalize it to x-a and recover a root.

items.title: The formal derivative of a polynomial
items.strategy: For f=sum a_i x^i, define f' by giving the coefficient of x^(i-1) as the ring multiple i a_i for positive i. State the constant and zero cases and use numerals as ring multiples, never an applied canonical-embedding notation.

items.title: Linearity, power rule, Leibniz rule and the degree bound for the formal derivative
items.strategy: Compare coefficients to prove additivity and the monomial power rule. For the product rule, reindex the convolution and split the coefficient multiplier i+j into its two additive parts. Inspect the support formula to prove that a nonzero derivative has degree strictly below that of the original nonconstant polynomial.

items.title: Repeated roots in extension fields and separable polynomials
items.strategy: For a field F contained as a subfield of E and nonzero f in F[x], call a in E a repeated root when (x-a)^2 divides f in E[x]. Call f separable over F when it has no repeated root in any extension field, and record the constant-polynomial convention.

items.title: A root is repeated exactly when it is also a root of the formal derivative
items.strategy: Differentiate f=(x-a)q to get f'=q+(x-a)q'. If f is divisible by (x-a)^2, both evaluations vanish. Conversely, f(a)=f'(a)=0 first gives f=(x-a)q and then q(a)=0, so the factor theorem gives a second factor x-a.

items.title: The monic gcd of two base-field polynomials is unchanged after extending the coefficient field
items.strategy: Factor out the base-field gcd and use its Bézout identity to show the remaining factors stay coprime over the extension. Hence no new positive-degree common factor appears; monic normalization fixes the associate.

items.title: A nonzero polynomial over a field is separable exactly when its gcd with its derivative is 1
items.strategy: If a repeated root occurs in an extension, the derivative criterion and gcd stability show the base gcd is nontrivial. Conversely, if the gcd has an irreducible factor p, pass to the field F[x]/(p), first checking that the constant-polynomial map embeds F because p is nonconstant; the residue class of x is then a common root of f and f', hence a repeated root.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial over a field is separable exactly when its derivative is nonzero
items.strategy: For irreducible f, any monic gcd of f and f' is 1 or the monic associate of f. Since deg f'<deg f whenever f' is nonzero, the second case occurs exactly when f'=0; apply the separability criterion.

items.title: Content and primitive integer polynomials
items.strategy: Use the unique trimmed coefficient list and define its finite gcd recursively from the published binary integer gcd, starting with 0; for a nonzero integer polynomial this gives a positive content. Call the polynomial primitive when its content is 1, separate the sign into a unit, and state the convention for nonzero constant polynomials.

items.title: Content is the positive common divisor of the coefficients divisible by every common divisor
items.strategy: Induct along the trimmed coefficient list using the published binary-gcd characterization. Prove that the recursive gcd divides every coefficient and that every common divisor of all coefficients divides it; for a nonzero polynomial it is positive. If the polynomial is not primitive, apply integer unique factorisation to obtain a prime divisor of its content and hence of every coefficient.

items.title: The product of primitive integer polynomials is primitive, and contents multiply
items.strategy: If a prime divided every coefficient of a product of two primitive polynomials, reduce modulo that prime and use that the polynomial ring over the resulting field is a domain. Then factor out the positive contents and compare signs to obtain c(fg)=c(f)c(g).

items.title: Gauss lemma: primitive factorisations over Q can be cleared to primitive factorisations over Z
items.strategy: Clear denominators from a rational factorization, extract positive contents from the resulting integer factors, and use content multiplicativity plus primitivity of f to cancel the scalar. Conclude that a primitive integer polynomial is irreducible over Q exactly when it is irreducible over Z.

items.title: Rational root theorem
items.strategy: Write a rational root in lowest terms as p/q with q positive. Multiply f(p/q)=0 by q^n; the coprime-divides-product lemma shows p divides the constant coefficient and q divides the leading coefficient. Include constant-zero and monic specializations without applying a canonical embedding to an index.

items.title: Irreducibility after reduction modulo a prime implies irreducibility over Q when the leading coefficient survives
items.strategy: For a primitive integer polynomial whose leading coefficient is not divisible by prime p, any rational factorization clears by Gauss to an integer factorization. Reduction modulo p preserves the degrees of both factors and contradicts irreducibility of the reduced polynomial.

items.title: Eisenstein criterion over the integers
items.strategy: Assume a primitive integer polynomial has leading coefficient not divisible by p, all lower coefficients divisible by p, and constant coefficient not divisible by p^2. Clear a hypothetical rational factorization by Gauss, reduce modulo p to force both positive-degree factors to have constant terms divisible by p, and contradict the constant coefficient condition.

items.title: For every prime p and positive n, x^n-p is irreducible over Q
items.strategy: Apply Eisenstein at p: the leading coefficient is 1, every lower nonconstant coefficient is 0, and the constant coefficient -p is divisible by p but not p^2. Check n=1 explicitly.

items.title: Formal polynomials are not the functions they induce
items.strategy: Explain that equality in R[x] is coefficientwise, while evaluation produces a function only after choosing a target ring. Over an infinite domain evaluation is injective by the root bound, but over finite rings distinct polynomials can induce the same function, as the companion counterexample shows.

pages.title: Polynomial Rings and Roots: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Polynomial addition and multiplication computed from coefficient convolution
items.strategy: Represent two explicit low-degree polynomials by coefficient sequences, compute their coordinatewise sum and each convolution coefficient, and verify the familiar expanded product without treating x as a variable value.

items.title: Long division, the Euclidean algorithm and a Bézout identity in Q[x]
items.strategy: Choose an explicit pair of rational polynomials, carry out successive divisions to the last nonzero remainder, normalize the gcd to monic, and back-substitute to display concrete Bézout coefficients.

items.title: Over Z/4, a nonconstant polynomial can be a unit and product degree can drop
items.strategy: In (Z/4)[x], compute (1+2x)^2=1. Thus 1+2x is its own inverse even though it is nonconstant, and two degree-one factors have a degree-zero product because the top coefficient 4 vanishes.

items.title: Division with a degree-small remainder can fail over Z when the divisor's leading coefficient is not a unit
items.strategy: Try to divide the constant polynomial 1 by the constant nonunit 2 in Z[x]. A remainder of degree below 0 must be zero, which would require 1=2q for an integer polynomial q, an impossibility.

items.title: Quadratics can have four roots over Z/6 and Z/8
items.strategy: Over Z/6, check that x^2-x vanishes at 0, 1, 3 and 4; over Z/8, check that x^2-1 vanishes at 1, 3, 5 and 7. These witnesses isolate the missing domain hypothesis in the root bound while the factor theorem remains valid.

items.title: Over F_p, x^p-x and the zero polynomial induce the same function but are distinct polynomials
items.strategy: Use Fermat's little theorem to show a^p-a=0 for every residue class a modulo prime p, while the coefficient of x^p proves that x^p-x is not the zero polynomial. Include p=2 and the positive-degree boundary explicitly.

items.title: The polynomial x^2-2 is irreducible over Q
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime, hence its integer divisors are exactly plus or minus 1 and plus or minus 2. The rational-root theorem restricts a rational root to those four candidates; direct evaluation excludes them, and the quadratic criterion gives irreducibility.

items.title: The polynomial x^2+1 is irreducible over R
items.strategy: The ordered-field laws give a^2>=0 for every real a, so a^2+1 is positive and never zero. Apply the quadratic criterion, without making any assertion here about factorisation over the complex numbers.

items.title: Reduction modulo 2 proves x^3+17x+391 irreducible over Q
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime. Reduce to x^3+x+1 over F_2, check its two possible values are nonzero, use the cubic criterion for irreducibility over F_2, and apply the reduction theorem.

items.title: Eisenstein proves x^n-2 irreducible over Q for every positive n
items.strategy: First check from the integer divisor bound and discreteness that 2 is prime. Then verify the Eisenstein hypotheses at 2 uniformly for positive n, including n=1, and apply the criterion.

items.title: Translation turns x^4+1 into an Eisenstein polynomial
items.strategy: Use the polynomial universal property to show substitution x->x+1 is an automorphism with inverse x->x-1. Expand (x+1)^4+1 and apply Eisenstein at 2, then transport irreducibility back to x^4+1.

items.title: A degree-four polynomial can be reducible over Q without having a rational root
items.strategy: Factor x^4+3x^2+2=(x^2+1)(x^2+2) in Q[x]. Since a rational square is nonnegative, neither quadratic factor has a rational root, so the product has none despite being reducible.

items.title: In characteristic 2, x^2+1=(x+1)^2 has zero derivative and a repeated root
items.strategy: Work in (Z/2)[x], compute the square and the formal derivative coefficientwise, and check the derivative criterion at the root 1.

items.title: For a field F, the ideal (x,y) in F[x,y] is not principal
items.strategy: If (x,y)=(d), then d divides both x and y. Compare degrees in each indeterminate to show every common divisor is a unit; that would make the ideal the whole ring, contradicted by evaluation at x=y=0.

pages.title: The Field of Fractions and Localisation
The Field of Fractions and Localisation: Examples and Counterexamples
Simple Field Extensions and the Construction of the Complex Numbers

items.title: Field extensions, generated subrings $F[S]$, generated subfields $F(S)$, and simple extensions
The composite of two subfields is the subfield generated by their union
items.strategy: For subfields $E,E'\subseteq\Omega$, apply the minimality clause for generated subfields to $E(E')$ and $E'(E)$. Each is the intersection of exactly the subfields of $\Omega$ containing both $E$ and $E'$, so they agree with each other and with the subfield generated by $E\cup E'$; denote this common field by $EE'$.

items.title: Algebraic and transcendental elements and algebraic extensions
The evaluation kernel and the unique monic irreducible minimal polynomial of an algebraic element
items.strategy: Use the polynomial-ring universal property to make evaluation an $F$-algebra homomorphism. Algebraicity is exactly nonzero kernel; principality gives a monic generator $m_\alpha$, minimal degree makes it irreducible, and membership in the kernel gives the divisibility characterization and uniqueness. Treat the transcendental case as the zero-kernel alternative.

items.title: A simple transcendental extension consists exactly of rational expressions in its generator
items.strategy:
Let $a$ be transcendental over $F$. The zero-kernel case of evaluation makes $F[x]	o F[a]$ injective, so $g
e0$ implies $g(a)
e0$. Prove directly that $R=\{f(a)g(a)^{-1}:f,g\in F[x],\ g
e0\}$ contains $F$ and $a$ and is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and inverses of nonzero elements. Thus $R$ is a subfield of the ambient extension containing $F$ and $a$; conversely every such subfield contains every displayed expression, so minimality gives $R=F(a)$. No field-of-fractions construction or notation is used.

items.title: Two simple transcendental extensions are uniquely $F$-isomorphic once their generators are matched
items.strategy: For transcendental $a$ and $b$, send $f(a)g(a)^{-1}$ to $f(b)g(b)^{-1}$. If two expressions agree at $a$, cross-multiplication and injectivity of evaluation at $a$ give equality of the corresponding polynomials in $F[x]$, hence equality after evaluation at $b$; this proves well-definedness. The same formula respects the field operations, and swapping $a,b$ gives its inverse. Every element has the preceding rational-expression form, which also forces uniqueness among $F$-homomorphisms sending $a$ to $b$.

items.title: $F[x]/(p)$ for monic irreducible $p$ is a field extension containing the root $x+(p)$ with unique reduced representatives
items.strategy: Apply the published irreducible-quotient criterion for fieldness. Prove that constants embed injectively by comparing degrees, set $a=x+(p)$, evaluate $p(a)=0$, and use polynomial division to give each coset a unique representative of degree below $\deg p$, including the constant and linear boundary cases.

items.title: Every nonconstant polynomial over a field has a root in some field extension
items.strategy: Factor the polynomial into irreducibles and choose one irreducible factor $p$. The quotient $F[x]/(p)$ is a field extension in which $a=x+(p)$ is a root of $p$, and therefore is a root of the original polynomial. Normalize $p$ to monic without changing its principal ideal, and exclude the zero polynomial through the nonconstant hypothesis.

items.title: Universal property of adjoining a root of an irreducible polynomial
items.strategy: For monic irreducible $p\in F[x]$, let $a=x+(p)$. Given an extension $L/F$ and $b\in L$ with $p(b)=0$, evaluation at $b$ kills $(p)$ and therefore factors uniquely through $F[x]/(p)$; the factor fixes $F$ and sends $a$ to $b$. Conversely those two requirements determine it because every quotient class is a polynomial in $a$.

items.title: A simple algebraic extension is its minimal-polynomial quotient and has power basis $1,a,\ldots,a^{n-1}$ and degree $n$
items.strategy: For algebraic $a$ with minimal polynomial $m_a$ of degree $n$, evaluation has kernel $(m_a)$ and image $F[a]$. The first isomorphism theorem identifies $F[x]/(m_a)$ with $F[a]$; fieldness makes $F[a]=F(a)$, and unique degree-below-$n$ representatives give unique coordinates in the displayed powers. Define $[F(a):F]=n$ here by that unique-coordinate basis, without importing the later general vector-space dimension theory.

items.title: Stem fields of a monic irreducible polynomial are uniquely $F$-isomorphic when their distinguished roots are matched
items.strategy: Let $L=F(\alpha)$ and $M=F(\beta)$ with $p(\alpha)=p(\beta)=0$. The minimal polynomials of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ divide the monic irreducible polynomial $p$, hence equal $p$. Use the quotient description and the root-adjunction universal property to obtain $F$-homomorphisms $L\to M$ and $M\to L$ carrying the distinguished roots to one another. Each composite fixes $F$ and its distinguished generator, so the uniqueness clause makes both composites identities; it also makes the resulting isomorphism unique.

items.title: $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: Every real square is nonnegative, so $r^2+1>0$ for every real $r$ and the polynomial has no real root. Invoke the degree-two irreducibility test, without any appeal to the fundamental theorem of algebra.

items.title: The complex numbers as $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$, with the real embedding and imaginary unit $i$
$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field, every element is uniquely $a+bi$, and every nonzero element has inverse $(a-bi)/(a^2+b^2)$
items.strategy: Apply the irreducible-quotient construction to obtain a field and unique linear representatives, then compute the induced addition and multiplication formulas using $i^2=-1$. For $a+bi\ne0$, ordered-field square positivity gives $a^2+b^2>0$, and direct multiplication verifies the displayed inverse; the remaining field axioms are inherited from the quotient ring, so none is merely asserted.

items.title: $\mathbb C$ is the real coordinate plane, with coordinate arithmetic and the Cartesian modulus formula
items.strategy: Define $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R^2$ by $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$. The unique coordinate form from the preceding field theorem makes $\Phi$ well-defined and bijective, and its addition and multiplication formulas give $\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$ and $\Phi((a+bi)(u+vi))=(au-bv,av+bu)$. Since $a^2+b^2\ge0$ and the reals form a complete ordered field, the real square-root theorem licenses the coordinate modulus definition $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Do not identify this formula with the Euclidean norm or the metric $d_2$ here; that comparison remains at order 189.

items.title: $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ has power basis $1,i$ and degree $2$
items.strategy: Specialize the power-basis theorem to the minimal polynomial $x^2+1$ of $i$ and identify the resulting unique coordinates with the already established form $a+bi$.

items.title: A square root of $-1$ in a real field extension determines a unique real-field homomorphism from $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Specialize the universal property of adjoining an irreducible root to $p=x^2+1$: an element $j$ with $j^2=-1$ is precisely a root, so there is a unique homomorphism fixing $\mathbb R$ and sending $i$ to $j$.

items.title: Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus
Conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, and modulus is definite, multiplicative, and subadditive
items.strategy: Compute conjugation on the unique coordinates $a+bi$ to prove its additive, multiplicative, involutive, and real-fixing laws. The norm identity gives definiteness and multiplicativity after uniqueness of nonnegative square roots. For the triangle inequality, expand the squared sides and use $(av-bu)^2\ge0$ to prove $(au+bv)^2\le(a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)$, then apply monotonicity of squaring on nonnegative reals.

items.title: The only real-field automorphisms of $\mathbb C$ are the identity and complex conjugation
items.strategy: A real-field automorphism sends $i$ to a root of $x^2+1$. Factor $z^2+1=(z-i)(z+i)$ in the complex field to show those roots are exactly $i$ and $-i$; unique $a+bi$ coordinates then force the automorphism to be respectively the identity or conjugation, both of which have already been verified.

items.title: Every complex number has a square root, by an explicit Cartesian formula
items.strategy: For $z=a+bi$, put $r=|z|$. Treat $z=0$ and the nonpositive-real axis separately. Otherwise set $u=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}>0$ and $v=b/(2u)$; use $r^2=a^2+b^2$ to obtain $v^2=(r-a)/2$, so $(u+vi)^2=a+bi$. This uses only real square roots and ordered-field algebra, never the fundamental theorem of algebra or polar form.

pages.title: Field Extensions and the Complex Numbers: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-2)$ with basis $1,\sqrt2$
items.strategy: Use Eisenstein at $2$ to identify $x^2-2$ as the minimal polynomial, then specialize the quotient and power-basis theorems and compute the inverse of a sample nonzero element by rationalizing inside the field.

items.title: The four-element field $(\mathbb Z/2)[x]/(x^2+x+1)$
items.strategy: Check that the quadratic has no root in $\mathbb Z/2$, apply the irreducible quotient construction, list the four reduced representatives $0,1,a,1+a$, and compute their multiplication from $a^2=a+1$ in characteristic two.

items.title: $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-1)$ is not a field: reducibility creates nonzero zero divisors
items.strategy: The nonzero classes of $x-1$ and $x+1$ multiply to zero because $(x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1$; degree comparison proves neither factor lies in the quotient ideal, isolating irreducibility in the quotient-field theorem.

items.title: The minimal polynomial of $\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $x^4-4x^2+1$
items.strategy: Successive squaring proves the element is a root. Translate the polynomial by $x\mapsto x+1$ to get $x^4+4x^3+2x^2-4x-2$, apply Eisenstein at $2$, and transport irreducibility back through the inverse translation; the minimal-polynomial theorem then identifies it and gives degree four.

items.title: The square roots of $i$ are $\pm(1+i)/\sqrt2$
items.strategy: Square the two displayed candidates using Cartesian multiplication and $(\sqrt2)^2=2$. Conversely compare real and imaginary parts of $(a+bi)^2=i$ to get $a^2=b^2=1/2$ and $ab=1/2$, forcing equal signs and exactly the two candidates.

items.title: FALSE: the complex field admits an order making it an ordered field
items.strategy: In any ordered field every nonzero square is positive, so both $1$ and $i^2$ would be positive; but $i^2=-1$, contradicting trichotomy or positivity of $1$. Thus no order compatible with the complex field operations exists.

items.title: An annihilating polynomial need not be minimal: $\sqrt2$ is a root of both $x^2-2$ and $x^4-4$
items.strategy: Evaluate both polynomials at $\sqrt2$ and factor $x^4-4=(x^2-2)(x^2+2)$. Eisenstein makes $x^2-2$ irreducible, so the evaluation-kernel theorem identifies it as the minimal polynomial and displays the larger annihilator as a proper multiple.

pages.title: Free Groups and Presentations — Examples

items.title: Reducing the word $xx^{-1}yy^{-1}x$ leaves the reduced word $x$

pages.title: Free Products and Amalgamation

items.title: The free product of an arbitrary family of groups
items.strategy: Define a free product by its coproduct universal property: compatible data are arbitrary homomorphisms from every factor to one target, with one unique mediating homomorphism. Do not assume the structure maps inject until normal form proves it.

items.title: Reduced syllable words in a family of groups
items.strategy: A syllable is a tagged nonidentity element of one factor. Define a reduced word as a finite syllable list whose adjacent tags differ; the empty word is allowed. Specify elementary multiplication by combining adjacent syllables from the same factor and deleting identities.

items.title: Factor elements act by mutually inverse permutations on reduced syllable words
items.strategy: For g in a factor, define left action on a reduced word by prepending g unless the first syllable lies in the same factor, in which case multiply and delete an identity result. Check all seam cases and prove the action for g^{-1} is inverse. Show each factor map into the permutation group is a homomorphism.

items.title: Reduced syllable words form the free product of a family of groups
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to define multiplication as successive action on the empty word and to separate distinct reduced words. Alternatively describe concatenation followed by seam reduction, then prove associativity through the permutation representation. Evaluate syllables in any target to obtain the unique mediating homomorphism, including the empty family.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products
items.strategy: Identify the constructed free product with its underlying reduced-word set. Prove every element has one reduced syllable expression and that a nonempty reduced word is not the identity by applying its factor action to the empty word.

items.title: Finite-order elements of a free product are conjugate into factors
items.strategy: Represent a nonidentity element by its reduced syllable word and repeatedly conjugate away matching end-factor syllables until a conjugate is either one syllable or has first and last syllables in different factors. In the latter case every positive power is a nonempty reduced concatenation, so normal form gives infinite order. Hence every nonidentity finite-order element is conjugate to a nonidentity finite-order element of one factor. State the identity separately for a nonempty family and note that the empty-family case is vacuous in the nonidentity formulation.

items.title: The center of a free product with at least two nontrivial factors is trivial
items.strategy: Let z be a nonidentity central element with reduced word x_1...x_n. Choose a nonidentity syllable g from a factor different from the factor of x_1. Then gz is reduced of length n+1. If the last syllable of z lies in g's factor, zg reduces to length at most n; otherwise zg is reduced of length n+1 but starts in a different factor from gz. Normal-form uniqueness gives gz not equal to zg, a contradiction. The identity is central, and the hypothesis supplies the required choice of g even when some other factors are trivial.

items.title: Every canonical factor map into a free product is injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity factor element is a one-syllable reduced word, hence is nonidentity by normal form. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and include the trivial-factor case.

items.title: Free products are unique up to a unique factor-compatible isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the two universal properties to obtain maps in both directions. Uniqueness makes both composites the identity because they agree with every factor map. Handle the empty family, whose free product is trivial.

items.title: Each factor is a retract of a free product when all other factors are sent trivially
items.strategy: Fix one index. Use the identity on that factor and trivial homomorphisms on all other factors in the universal property, then compose with the injective canonical factor map. State the assertion only for an index belonging to the family.

items.title: A free product has the union presentation of presentations of its factors
items.strategy: After replacing generator alphabets by disjoint copies, show that the group presented by the union of all generators and factor relators has the free-product universal property. Use von Dyck to extend each family of factor maps and uniqueness on generators. Cover empty and singleton families.

items.title: Free groups on disjoint bases freely multiply to the free group on their union
items.strategy: For disjoint sets X_i, compare maps from the union to a target with families of maps from each X_i. The universal properties of the free groups and the free product give the same unique extension, so uniqueness identifies the two groups. Include empty bases and an empty family.

items.title: A free product of copies of the infinite cyclic group is a free group
items.strategy: For each tagged infinite cyclic factor C_i=<c_i>, use the description by integer powers, uniqueness of exponents, and the exponent-addition law to prove directly that (C_i,{x_i}->C_i) satisfies the free-group universal property on the singleton {x_i}. Make the singleton bases disjoint and apply the disjoint-basis theorem. Preserve the arbitrary index set and its empty case.

items.title: The free product of two infinite cyclic groups is the free group on two generators
items.strategy: Specialise the preceding arbitrary-family result to two singleton bases and use the finite-rank definition. Record the compatible images of the two standard generators.

items.title: Pushouts of group homomorphisms
items.strategy: For homomorphisms f:K to G and h:K to H, define a group pushout by the commuting-square universal property. Do not build injectivity into the definition and explicitly allow arbitrary, noninjective homomorphisms.

items.title: A group pushout is the quotient of a free product by the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Form G*H and quotient by the normal closure of f(k)h(k)^{-1} for k in K. The quotient maps agree on K. Given any compatible pair of maps, free-product universality supplies a map that kills those relators, so quotient universality gives the unique mediator. Include K, G, or H trivial and arbitrary kernels.

items.title: Free products with amalgamation along monomorphisms
items.strategy: When f:K to G and h:K to H are injective, call their group pushout the free product with amalgamation G *_K H. Explain that the notation identifies K with its two images only after the embedding theorem is proved.

items.title: A free product with amalgamation has the factor presentations plus the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Take disjoint presentations of G and H, use their union presentation for G*H, and add relations identifying a chosen generating set of K through the two monomorphisms. Prove the resulting presentation has the pushout universal property and explain why using all k in K gives the same normal closure.

items.title: Transversal normal-form data for an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: After identifying K with subgroups of G and H provisionally, choose left-coset transversals S_G,S_H containing the identity. Define normal words s_1...s_n k with nonidentity representatives alternating between transversals and k in K. Record length zero and the dependence of the written representative on the transversal choices.

items.title: Factor elements act consistently by permutations on amalgamated normal words
items.strategy: Following Schreier's permutation proof, define P_g(w) by multiplying the terminal K coefficient on the right by g^{-1}, rewriting uniquely with the selected left-coset transversal, and merging with the last syllable when it comes from the same factor. Check P_{gh}=P_g composed with P_h under the library's composition convention, prove inverses act inversely, and prove that the two factor actions agree on K.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products with amalgamation
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to realise the presented amalgamated product as permutations of its normal-word set. Show every element has a unique form s_1...s_n k and that a positive-length normal word is nonidentity. Prove independence of the chosen transversals through the pushout universal property, while retaining the length-zero K case.

items.title: The factor maps into a free product with amalgamation are injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity element of either factor has either a nontrivial K coefficient or a one-syllable normal form, so it cannot map to the identity. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and keep the trivial factor and K=G boundary cases.

items.title: The two factor images intersect exactly in the amalgamated subgroup
items.strategy: The amalgamated K-image lies in both factors. Conversely, if images of g in G and h in H agree, the normal form of gh^{-1} can be trivial only when both elements represent the same element of K. Include K trivial and K equal to one factor.

items.title: Amalgamation over the trivial group is the ordinary free product
items.strategy: For the two maps from the trivial group, the compatibility condition is automatic, so the pushout and free-product universal properties coincide. Use uniqueness to obtain the canonical isomorphism and check trivial factors.

items.title: The kernels of the amalgamating maps are killed in the opposite canonical maps to a group pushout
items.strategy: If k lies in ker f, commutativity gives i_H(h(k))=i_G(e)=e; symmetrically i_G(f(ker h)) is trivial. Deduce that injectivity of a canonical factor map can fail for arbitrary pushout data and identify the exact kernel containment without claiming equality.

items.title: A pushout along an isomorphism is isomorphic to the other factor
items.strategy: When f:K to G is an isomorphism, use h composed with f^{-1}:G to H and the identity of H as a compatible cocone. Verify the universal property and obtain the unique isomorphism. Treat trivial groups without a separate argument.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for free products and amalgamation
items.strategy: Record that free products allow arbitrary index sets; group pushouts allow arbitrary homomorphisms; the notation G *_K H and the normal-form, embedding, and intersection theorems require monomorphisms. State that HNN extensions, Kurosh's subgroup theorem, Grushko's theorem, and Bass-Serre theory are not claimed from this page's declared prerequisites.

pages.title: Free Products and Amalgamation — Examples

items.title: C_2 free-product C_2 is the infinite dihedral group, and the product of its generators has infinite order
items.strategy: Use the union presentation to obtain generators s,t with s^2=t^2=e. Normal form shows every positive power of st is a nonempty reduced word, so st has infinite order. Identify this presentation as the standard infinite dihedral group convention.

items.title: C_2 free-product C_3 has presentation with only the two factor relations and is infinite
items.strategy: The presentation theorem gives <s,t | s^2, t^3>. The words (st)^n are distinct reduced normal forms for nonnegative n, proving infinitude without importing the modular-group identification.

items.title: The canonical surjection from a free product to the direct product of its factors
items.strategy: Map G to G times H by g to (g,e) and H by h to (e,h), then use free-product universality. These images generate the direct product, so the induced map is surjective. Show every cross-commutator lies in its kernel and give nontrivial factors for which normal form makes such a commutator nonidentity.

items.title: FALSE: a free product of abelian groups is abelian
items.strategy: In C_2*C_2 the reduced words st and ts are distinct. Thus the two canonical generators do not commute even though both factors are abelian.

items.title: Amalgamating infinite cyclic groups by multiplication by m and n gives the presentation with relation x^m=y^n
items.strategy: For positive m,n, realise each factor as the one-generator word-quotient free group. Its normal form shows that it is infinite cyclic, and the free-group theorem together with the presentation definition and the empty normal closure gives its empty-relator presentation. Apply the amalgamated-presentation theorem to the injective maps taking the edge generator to x^m and y^n. The amalgam normal form embeds both cyclic factors. Specialise to m=2,n=3 without asserting the torus-knot interpretation.

items.title: Amalgamating C_2 inside C_4 and C_6 gives the presentation with a^2=b^3
items.strategy: Embed C_2 as the unique order-two subgroup in each cyclic factor. The presentation is <a,b | a^4, b^6, a^2=b^3>. Apply embedding and intersection corollaries to verify that the factor images remain C_4 and C_6 and meet in precisely C_2.

items.title: FALSE: canonical factor maps into every group pushout are injective
items.strategy: Take the maps from C_2 to the trivial group and to C_2, the first trivial and the second the identity. The pushout is trivial by its universal property, so the canonical map from the second C_2 is not injective. Relate this directly to kernel collapse.

items.title: A pushout along an isomorphism recovers the other group
items.strategy: For an isomorphism K to G and any homomorphism K to H, construct the pushout as H. Work one concrete cyclic case and check both legs and the unique mediator rather than appealing only to the slogan.

pages.title: Conjugacy in $S_n$, Generation, and the Simplicity of $A_n$

items.title: Conjugating a cycle relabels each entry: $g(a_1\,\ldots\,a_k)g^{-1}=(g(a_1)\,\ldots\,g(a_k))$
items.strategy: Evaluate the conjugate at each relabelled cycle point and at every point outside their set. The first calculation advances one position and the second fixes the point, which proves equality as permutations rather than merely agreement on the displayed support.

items.title: Two elements of $S_n$ are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type
items.strategy: Conjugate a disjoint-cycle decomposition factor by factor using the relabelling lemma, proving invariance of cycle type. Conversely align equally long cycles, including fixed points, and define one bijection sending their entries positionwise; the same lemma shows it conjugates the first permutation to the second.

items.title: The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are indexed by the tuples $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with $\sum k c_k=n$
items.strategy: The cycle-type definition gives exactly one such multiplicity tuple for each permutation, and the conjugacy classification says two permutations give the same tuple exactly when they lie in the same conjugacy class. Construct a representative from disjoint cycles for every admissible tuple, including $n=0$.

items.title: If $\sigma\in S_n$ has $c_k$ cycles of length $k$, then $|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_{k=1}^n k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: A commuting permutation must send each $\langle\sigma\rangle$-orbit to another orbit of the same length. For the $c_k$ length-$k$ orbits, choose an arbitrary permutation of those orbits and an independent cyclic offset on each, giving $c_k!k^{c_k}$ choices; prove these choices assemble uniquely and multiply independently across lengths. Check $c_k=0$, the identity, and $n=0$ via empty products.

items.title: The class equation of $S_n$ is $n!=\sum_{\sum k c_k=n} n!/\prod_k k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: Index the conjugacy classes by cycle-type tuples, combine conjugacy-class cardinality with the centralizer formula, and sum the disjoint class sizes. At $n=0$ the single empty type contributes $1$.

items.title: $Z(S_n)$ is trivial for $n\ge3$
items.strategy: A central permutation has a singleton conjugacy class, hence its cycle type has class-size formula $1$. Show every nonidentity cycle type for $n\ge3$ has more than one relabelling, or directly choose a transposition whose conjugation changes a moved point; conclude only the identity is central. Record the exceptional abelian groups $S_0,S_1,S_2$.

items.title: The adjacent transpositions $(1\,2),(2\,3),\ldots,(n-1\,n)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Express every transposition $(a\,b)$ with $a<b$ as the standard palindromic word in adjacent transpositions, checking the word pointwise. Since all transpositions generate $S_n$, so do the adjacent ones; include $n=0,1$ as empty generating sets for the trivial groups.

items.title: For $n\ge2$, $(1\,2\,\ldots\,n)$ and $(1\,2)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by successive powers of the $n$-cycle produces every neighboring transposition around the cycle, in particular the standard adjacent transpositions. Apply adjacent generation; at $n=2$ the two displayed generators coincide and still generate $S_2$.

items.title: $A_n$ is generated by $3$-cycles for every $n\ge3$
items.strategy: Write an even permutation as a product of an even number of transpositions and pair them. Equal pairs cancel, overlapping pairs are one $3$-cycle, and disjoint pairs are a product of two $3$-cycles by explicit identities; hence every even permutation lies in the subgroup generated by $3$-cycles, while every $3$-cycle is even.

items.title: A conjugacy class in an index-two normal subgroup remains one class or splits into two equal classes, with a centralizer criterion
items.strategy: For $H\trianglelefteq G$ of index two and $x\in H$, write $G=H\sqcup tH$. Then $\operatorname{Cl}_G(x)$ is the union of the $H$-class of $x$ and its $t$-conjugate. The two classes agree exactly when some element outside $H$ centralizes $x$; otherwise they are disjoint and conjugation by $t$ bijects them, giving equal size.

items.title: An $S_n$-class of an even permutation splits in $A_n$ exactly when all cycle lengths, including $1$-cycles, are odd and distinct
items.strategy: Use the index-two splitting lemma with $H=A_n$. An even-length cycle is itself an odd centralizer element; two equal odd-length cycles can be swapped by an odd permutation, including two fixed points. Conversely, when the lengths are distinct and odd, every centralizer element preserves each cycle support and restricts there to a power of that odd cycle, hence is even. This proves both directions and the equal-size conclusion.

items.title: All $3$-cycles are conjugate in $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: They have common cycle type $(3,1^{n-3})$. The splitting criterion does not split that type when $n\ge5$ because the fixed-point length $1$ is repeated; equivalently correct an odd $S_n$ conjugator by a transposition on two fixed points.

items.title: Simple groups
A normal subgroup of $A_n$ containing one $3$-cycle equals $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Normality contains the whole $A_n$-conjugacy class of the given $3$-cycle. All $3$-cycles form that one class for $n\ge5$, and the separate generation theorem says they generate $A_n$.

items.title: Every nontrivial normal subgroup of $A_n$ contains a $3$-cycle for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Choose a nonidentity element of the normal subgroup with maximal number of fixed points. If it is not a $3$-cycle, split its cycle structure into the two exhaustive regimes: it has a cycle of length at least three with additional moved points, or it is a product of disjoint transpositions. In each regime choose a $3$-cycle $g$ so the nonidentity commutator $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$ lies in the subgroup but fixes strictly more points, a contradiction. Verify separately the $4$-cycle and two-transposition edge configurations and the availability of a fifth point.

items.title: $A_n$ is simple for every $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Let $N\trianglelefteq A_n$. If $N$ is nontrivial, the preceding support-reduction lemma supplies a $3$-cycle, and the normal-subgroup lemma then gives $N=A_n$. Exhibit two noncommuting $3$-cycles to ensure $A_n$ is nontrivial and nonabelian under the stated convention for simple groups.

items.title: For $n\ge5$, the only proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $S_n$ is $A_n$
items.strategy: For $N\trianglelefteq S_n$, simplicity makes $N\cap A_n$ either trivial or all of $A_n$. The latter gives $N=A_n$ or $S_n$; in the former case sign is injective on $N$, so a nontrivial $N$ has order two and its unique nonidentity element is central in $S_n$, contradicting triviality of the center.

items.title: $[S_n,S_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge2$, and $[A_n,A_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Because sign has abelian image, the quotient criterion puts $[S_n,S_n]$ inside $A_n$; every $3$-cycle is an explicit commutator of transpositions, so $3$-cycle generation gives the reverse inclusion. For $A_n$, its commutator subgroup is normal; two overlapping $3$-cycles do not commute, so it is nontrivial, and simplicity forces it to be all of $A_n$.

pages.title: Conjugacy in $S_n$, Generation, and the Simplicity of $A_n$ — Examples

items.title: Conjugating $(1\,4)(2\,5\,3)$ by an explicit permutation in $S_5$
items.strategy: Apply the relabelling formula cycle by cycle, then verify the result pointwise and read off that its cycle type is unchanged. Reverse the calculation to demonstrate the constructive direction of the conjugacy classification.

items.title: The five conjugacy classes of $S_4$ and the class equation $24=1+6+3+8+6$
items.strategy: List the five cycle types, compute each centralizer size from $\prod k^{c_k}c_k!$, divide $24$ by it, and sum the resulting class sizes. Include parity and representatives to prepare the $A_4$ examples.

items.title: The seven conjugacy classes of $S_5$ and their centralizer and class sizes
items.strategy: Enumerate the seven cycle types of five, tabulate $z_\lambda=\prod k^{c_k}c_k!$ and $120/z_\lambda$, and check that the class sizes sum to $120$; mark which types are even and which satisfy the alternating split criterion.

items.title: The conjugacy classes of $A_5$: sizes $1,20,15,12,12$ and the split $5$-cycles
items.strategy: Restrict the even $S_5$ cycle types. The identity, $3$-cycles, and double transpositions remain single classes; the distinct odd type $(5)$ splits into two classes of size $12$. Exhibit representatives from the two $5$-cycle classes and verify the total is $60$.

items.title: $V_4=\{1,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $A_4$
items.strategy: Verify closure directly and note that conjugation relabels a double transposition, so the displayed set is invariant under $A_4$ (indeed under $S_4$). Its order four is strictly between $1$ and $|A_4|=12$, making the counterexample explicit.

items.title: FALSE: two even permutations of the same cycle type are always conjugate in $A_n$
items.strategy: In $A_4$, the $S_4$-class of eight $3$-cycles has type $(3,1)$ and splits into two classes of four. Compute directly that every permutation conjugating $(123)$ to $(132)$ in $S_4$ is odd, so the two are not conjugate in $A_4$.

items.title: FALSE: $A_n$ is simple for every $n\ge4$
items.strategy: Use the explicitly verified subgroup $V_4\trianglelefteq A_4$, which is neither trivial nor all of $A_4$. Contrast this exact failure at $n=4$ with the theorem's valid boundary $n\ge5$.

items.title: FALSE: any transposition together with any $n$-cycle generates $S_n$
items.strategy: In $S_4$, the elements $(1234)$ and $(13)$ preserve the block system $\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}$, possibly swapping its two blocks, so their generated subgroup is proper. The example isolates why the main theorem requires a neighboring transposition relative to the chosen cycle.

items.title: Vector space over a field: an abelian group together with a scalar multiplication satisfying the four compatibility axioms
items.strategy: THREE THINGS THIS ITEM MUST GET RIGHT. (1) THE FIELD IS THE PUBLISHED ONE: cite [[def-field]] (order 9) and do not restate the field axioms. (2) THE ADDITIVE PART IS AN ABELIAN GROUP in the published sense of [[def-group]]: say so explicitly, so that associativity, commutativity, the uniqueness of $0_V$ ([[lem-identity-unique]]) and the uniqueness of $-v$ ([[lem-inverse-unique]]) are inherited and are never re-derived here. (3) SCALAR MULTIPLICATION IS NOT A BINARY OPERATION ON A SET: it is a map $F \times V \to V$, so [[def-binary-operation]] does not apply to it and must not be cited for it. State the four axioms as $\lambda(u+v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$, $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$, $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$ and $1_F v = v$, and note that the last is an axiom and not a consequence.

items.title: In any vector space $0_F v = 0_V$, $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$, $(-\lambda)v = -(\lambda v)$, $(-1_F)v = -v$, and $\lambda v = 0_V$ forces $\lambda = 0_F$ or $v = 0_V$
The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS: the pointwise rules are genuinely a map $F^{X} \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$ and a map $F \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$, and each axiom is checked pointwise from the field axioms. INDEX DISCIPLINE, and this is the single most likely defect on the page: a natural number here is a von Neumann natural, so $n = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]) and the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, NOT $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Every displayed tuple on this page and its companion must start at index $0$. State the two boundary cases: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, so it is the zero space; and $F^{1}$ is $F$ up to the obvious identification. DICTIONARY: the same set $F^{X}$ carries the ring structure of [[def-ring-of-functions]] (order 42), with the SAME addition and with pointwise multiplication in place of scalar multiplication; link that item in `## Remarks` and say which operation is which, so the two structures are never conflated.

items.title: The vector space $M_{m \times n}(F) := F^{\,m \times n}$ of $m$ by $n$ matrices over a field, with entrywise operations
items.strategy: This item introduces ONLY the vector-space structure and the notation $a_{ij}$; the matrix product, the ring $M_n(F)$ and the matrix of a linear map belong to order 74 and must NOT be anticipated here, not even in a remark that would need them. Index discipline as in [[def-function-space]]: rows are indexed by $i \in m = \{0,\dots,m-1\}$ and columns by $j \in n$, both starting at $0$.

items.title: A field is a vector space over itself, and over any subfield $K \subseteq F$ every $F$-vector space is a $K$-vector space by restricting the scalars
Linear subspace of a vector space
items.strategy: NAMING, decided at step 1 and to be honoured: the id says LINEAR subspace and the title says it too, because the library already uses "subspace" for the topological notion ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], order 185) and the two are unrelated. Do not link the topological item and do not remark on it; it is 117 pages later, so a link would be a forward reference needing declaration, and the qualified name is the whole fix. WELL-DEFINEDNESS: state that the restricted operations really are a vector addition and a scalar multiplication on $W$, and that $(W,+,0_V)$ is then a vector space whose zero and whose negatives are those of $V$ (that half is [[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]], proved next, and is cited rather than re-argued).

items.title: The additive group of a vector space is an abelian group and every linear subspace is a subgroup of it; conversely a subgroup closed under scalar multiplication is a linear subspace
One-step subspace test: a nonempty $W \subseteq V$ is a linear subspace if and only if $\lambda u + v \in W$ for all $\lambda \in F$ and $u, v \in W$
The intersection of a nonempty family of linear subspaces of $V$ is a linear subspace of $V$
Linear combination of a finite list, and the span $\operatorname{span}(S)$ as the smallest linear subspace containing $S$
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS, in the shape the published [[def-generated-subgroup]] already uses and which must be reused rather than invented: the family of linear subspaces containing $S$ is nonempty because $V$ belongs to it, so its intersection is a linear subspace by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]], and that intersection is the SMALLEST subspace containing $S$; those two properties determine it, which is what licenses the definite article. A linear combination is $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to V$, the sum being the finite product of the published [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian group $(V,+)$: cite it, do NOT define a new finite sum, and note that [[def-finite-sum]] is unavailable because it is stated for sequences into the complete ordered field. Index from $0$, and state that the empty combination ($n = 0$) is $0_V$, so $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ as a consequence and not as a stipulation.

items.title: $\operatorname{span}(S)$ is exactly the set of linear combinations of finite lists of elements of $S$, and $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
The span is monotone and idempotent, $\operatorname{span}(S) = S$ exactly when $S$ is a linear subspace, and $\operatorname{span}(S \cup \{0_V\}) = \operatorname{span}(S)$
$\operatorname{span}\{v\} = \{\, \lambda v : \lambda \in F \,\}$, which is $\{0_V\}$ when $v = 0_V$ and otherwise meets $\{0_V\}$ only there
The sum $U + W$ of two linear subspaces and the sum $\sum_{i<n} U_i$ of a finite family
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS AND BOUNDARY: the sum is defined as the set of all $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$, the finite sum again being [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively; the item must PROVE that this set is a linear subspace rather than assert it. Index from $0$, and state the empty case: the sum of the empty family ($n = 0$) is $\{0_V\}$, which is what makes the induction in [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]] start.

items.title: $\sum_{i<n} U_i = \operatorname{span}\bigl(\bigcup_{i<n} U_i\bigr)$, so the sum is the smallest linear subspace containing every $U_i$
Internal direct sum $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$: the sum is everything and each summand meets the sum of the others only in $0_V$
items.strategy: THE TRAP THIS ITEM EXISTS TO AVOID: for three or more summands, PAIRWISE trivial intersections are NOT sufficient, and the condition must be stated as $U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$ for every $j < n$. Writing the pairwise condition would make the definition false, and the companion page carries [[cex-pairwise-trivial-intersection-is-not-a-direct-sum]] as the witness. State the two-summand case explicitly as the familiar $V = U + W$ with $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and say that for two summands the two conditions do coincide. Index from $0$; the empty direct sum ($n = 0$) is the zero space.

items.title: $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$ if and only if every $v \in V$ is $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$ in exactly one way; equivalently, if and only if the sum is $V$ and $\sum_{i<n} u_i = 0_V$ with $u_i \in U_i$ forces every $u_i = 0_V$
