items.title: Two to the square root of two from rational suprema and from exp(sqrt(2) log 2)
The alternating harmonic series sums to log 2
Concrete logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential growth comparisons
x^x tends to one as x tends to zero from the right
The log(1+x) power series diverges at x=-1
The logarithm is not uniformly continuous on the positive half-line

pages.title: The Integral Logarithm and the Equivalence of Its Characterisations

items.title: The integral logarithm L(x):=integral from 1 to x of dt/t for x>0
The integral logarithm satisfies L'(x)=1/x for x>0 and L(1)=0
items.strategy: Choose a compact positive interval containing both x and 1. Additivity and the orientation convention rewrite L near x as a constant plus an integral function with a fixed lower endpoint, so the first FTC gives L'(x)=1/x on either side of 1. The oriented integral from 1 to 1 is zero. No exponential or logarithm result is cited.

items.title: The integral logarithm is continuous and strictly increasing on (0,infinity)
items.strategy: Differentiability gives continuity. For 0<a<b, the mean value theorem gives L(b)-L(a)=(b-a)/c for some c in (a,b), which is positive.

items.title: The integral logarithm satisfies L(xy)=L(x)+L(y) for all positive x and y
items.strategy: Fix y>0 and set h(x)=L(xy)-L(x). By the chain rule and L'=1/x, h'(x)=y/(xy)-1/x=0. The zero-derivative theorem makes h constant, and h(1)=L(y)-L(1)=L(y). This proof deliberately uses no substitution theorem and no exponential.

items.title: L(1/x)=-L(x), L(x^n)=nL(x), and in particular L(2^n)=nL(2)
items.strategy: Apply the product law to x(1/x)=1 for reciprocals and induct on the natural exponent for powers, with n=0 using L(1)=0. Negative integer powers follow from reciprocals. Since L is strictly increasing, L(2)>0.

items.title: The integral logarithm is unbounded above and below
items.strategy: Because L(2)>0, the Archimedean property makes nL(2) exceed any prescribed real bound. The power formula identifies this value with L(2^n), and the reciprocal formula gives L(2^{-n})=-nL(2) for the lower bound. No exponential is used.

items.title: L:(0,infinity) to R is a continuous strictly increasing bijection
items.strategy: Strict increase gives injectivity. For a target r, choose positive a<b with L(a)<r<L(b) using two-sided unboundedness, then apply the intermediate value theorem on [a,b] for surjectivity. Continuity comes from differentiability.

items.title: The integral exponential E:R to (0,infinity) as the inverse of L
The inverse E satisfies E(a+b)=E(a)E(b)
items.strategy: The product law gives L(E(a)E(b))=a+b=L(E(a+b)); injectivity of L gives the result. This remains entirely inside the integral construction.

items.title: The inverse E is differentiable, E'=E, and E(0)=1
items.strategy: Apply the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem to L at E(y): E'(y)=1/L'(E(y))=E(y). Since L(1)=0 and E is its inverse, E(0)=1. This proof contains no reference to the published exponential.

items.title: The integral exponential E is the published exponential function
items.strategy: The preceding theorem gives E'=E and E(0)=1. Invoke thm-exponential-ivp-uniqueness once to conclude E=exp. This is the sole bridge from the integral construction to exp.

items.title: The integral logarithm L is the published natural logarithm
items.strategy: L is the inverse of E, E=exp by the bridge theorem, and the published log is defined as exp^{-1}; uniqueness of inverse functions gives L=log.

items.title: The number e is the unique x>0 satisfying integral from 1 to x of dt/t=1
items.strategy: Since E=exp, E(1)=exp(1)=e. Inverse identities give L(e)=1, and strict increase of L gives uniqueness.

items.title: Log is the unique continuous f:(0,infinity) to R with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) and f(e)=1
items.strategy: Set g(t)=f(E(t)). The integral-exponential addition law makes g additive, and E is continuous because E is differentiable. Cauchy regularity gives g(t)=ct. The single bridge gives E(1)=exp(1)=e, so g(1)=f(e)=1 fixes c=1. For x>0, x=E(L(x)), hence f(x)=L(x)=log x. Conversely, the published log has the required law, continuity and normalisation.

items.title: Log is the unique f with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) that is differentiable at 1 with f'(1)=1
items.strategy: The functional equation gives f(1)=0. Rewriting f(x+h)-f(x)=f(1+h/x)-f(1) and scaling the difference quotient proves differentiability at every x with f'(x)=f'(1)/x=1/x. Therefore (f-L)'=0 and f(1)=L(1)=0, so f=L=log.

items.title: Every continuous f with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) is f(x)=c log x for a unique c, including c=0
items.strategy: Apply the same transport g=f composed with E. The addition law and continuity of E make g continuous and additive, so Cauchy regularity gives g(t)=ct with c=g(1)=f(e). For x>0, x=E(L(x)) gives f(x)=cL(x)=c log x. Uniqueness follows by evaluating at e. For c nonzero this is the constant-multiple form underlying logarithms to other bases; c=0 is the trivial solution and requires no division.

items.title: The Mercator series, its value at 1 and the product law determine log on all positive reals, while the series alone is only local
items.strategy: For every x>0, use the Archimedean property to choose a natural k with 0<x/2^k<2, then write x=2^k(1+u) with |u|<1. Any product-law function agreeing with the Mercator series on 1+u and at 2 must have f(x)=k f(2)+f(1+u), so at most one extension exists; the published log series and log laws supply existence. State explicitly that this is continuation data, not convergence of the original series at x-1.

items.title: Five characterisations of the natural logarithm are equivalent: inverse exponential, integral, continued Mercator series, Landau root limit and the normalised functional equation
items.strategy: Use the single E=exp bridge and inversion for the integral characterisation; cite the published Mercator and Landau theorems for their local or pointwise formulas; use the extension lemma to state exactly what extra product-law data makes the series global; and use the continuous functional-equation uniqueness theorem for the fifth characterisation. Distinguish full-domain definitions from the local series plus continuation rule.

items.title: Roadmap and non-circularity of the logarithm characterisations

pages.title: The Integral Logarithm and the Equivalence of Its Characterisations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Log 2 from four characterisations: hyperbolic area, the alternating harmonic series, Landau iterates and exp^{-1}(2)
items.strategy: List the four equal quantities integral_1^2 dt/t, sum_{n>=1}(-1)^{n+1}/n, lim 2^n(2^{1/2^n}-1), and the unique y with exp(y)=2. Cite the A-page series and Landau results directly, not the already-published B-page example, and identify all four through the equivalence theorem.

items.title: Dropping f(e)=1 leaves the whole family c log, including logarithms to other bases and the zero function
items.strategy: Verify directly that c log(xy)=c log x+c log y, compute f(e)=c, and compare c=1/log b with log_b for b>0, b not equal to 1. Include c=0 to show why the family is slightly larger than base logarithms.

items.title: Assuming choice, a Hamel-basis additive map transported through exp gives a discontinuous logarithmic function that is not c log
items.strategy: From a Hamel basis choose a coefficient map g:R->R that is additive and not scalar multiplication. Define f(exp t)=g(t), which is well-defined because exp is bijective. The exponential law gives f(xy)=f(x)+f(y). If f were continuous, then g=f composed with exp would be continuous and Cauchy regularity would force g to be scalar, a contradiction.

items.title: For every x>2 the uncontinued Mercator series at u=x-1 diverges
items.strategy: For u=x-1>1, the absolute ratio of successive terms u^n/n tends to u>1; the ratio test gives divergence (equivalently the terms do not tend to zero). Contrast this with the product-law continuation in the A-page lemma.

items.title: Integral bounds alone give 2<e<4; the sharper published bound is 2<e<3
items.strategy: Split [1,2] at 3/2. Monotonicity gives 7/12<=L(2)<=5/6, hence L(2)<1 and L(4)=2L(2)>1. Since L(e)=1 and L is strictly increasing, 2<e<4. Cite, but do not reprove, the sharper 2<e<3 corollary.

pages.title: Sine, Cosine, and the Definition of Pi

items.title: Sine and cosine defined by their real power series
The sine and cosine power series converge absolutely for every real argument
The derivatives of sine and cosine are cosine and minus sine

pages.title: Arc Length and Rectifiable Curves

items.title: Paths in $\mathbb{R}^n$, inscribed polygonal sums, arc length as their supremum, and rectifiability
Every endpoint chord is no longer than the arc: $\lVert\gamma(b)-\gamma(a)\rVert_2\le L(\gamma)$
items.strategy: Use the partition consisting only of the two endpoints. Its polygonal sum is the endpoint chord, and the defining supremum for arc length is at least every such sum. Include the singleton interval, where both sides are zero.

items.title: Refining a partition cannot decrease its inscribed polygonal length
items.strategy: It is enough to insert one new partition point. The old chord is no longer than the sum of the two replacement chords by the Euclidean triangle inequality; all other terms agree. Iterate over the finitely many inserted points, including a repeated insertion as a no-op.

items.title: A path in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is rectifiable exactly when every coordinate has bounded variation
items.strategy: For each partition, every scalar coordinate increment is bounded by the Euclidean chord, giving $\operatorname{Var}(\gamma_i)\le L(\gamma)$. Conversely the Euclidean chord is at most the sum of the absolute coordinate increments, so $L(\gamma)\le\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(\gamma_i)$. Take suprema and retain the singleton interval and $n=1$ cases explicitly.

items.title: Arc length is additive across every subdivision point and decreases under restriction
items.strategy: Splice partitions from the two adjacent subintervals to get one inequality. For the other, insert the subdivision point into an arbitrary partition, use refinement monotonicity, and split the resulting finite sum. Treat a subdivision at either endpoint through the zero-length singleton convention.

items.title: Arc length is invariant under every continuous surjective monotone reparametrization, including pauses and reversal
items.strategy: A monotone map sends a partition to an ordered list whose repetitions can be deleted without changing the polygonal sum, proving one inequality. Conversely choose ordered preimages of the finitely many points of any target partition; monotonicity makes them a partition of the source. Apply the same argument to nonincreasing maps after reversing the order, and include constant paths and singleton intervals.

items.title: A $C$-Lipschitz map multiplies path length by at most $C$; isometries preserve length and scalar dilation multiplies it by the absolute scale
items.strategy: Apply the Lipschitz inequality to each chord of each partition and take suprema. Apply the result in both directions for an isometry. For translation and orthogonal maps compute chord norms directly; for scalar dilation use homogeneity, including scale zero and a zero-length path.

items.title: Arc length is lower semicontinuous under uniform convergence of paths
items.strategy: Fix a finite partition. Uniform convergence gives convergence of the finitely many vertices and hence of that polygonal sum. Each approximating sum is bounded by the approximating path's length, so the limiting sum is bounded by the liminf of those lengths. Take the supremum over partitions only after this fixed-partition inequality.

items.title: If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $\gamma'$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, then $L(\gamma)=\int_a^b\lVert\gamma'(t)\rVert_2\,dt$
items.strategy: Vector Newton–Leibniz and the norm inequality bound every chord sum above by the speed integral. For the reverse bound, use uniform continuity of the extended derivative: on a fine partition, compare each derivative Riemann term with the corresponding chord through the integral of $\gamma'(t)-\gamma'(\xi_i)$, sum the uniform errors, and pass to the Riemann integral. State the endpoint-extension convention and singleton interval separately.

items.title: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, then the graph of $f$ has length $\int_a^b\sqrt{1+f'(t)^2}\,dt$
items.strategy: Apply the C1 path-length theorem to $\gamma(t)=(t,f(t))$. Componentwise differentiation gives the continuous derivative extension $(1,f'(t))$, and the Euclidean two-norm is $\sqrt{1+f'(t)^2}$. Retain the singleton-interval case separately.

items.title: A continuous piecewise-$C^1$ path is rectifiable and its length is the sum of the speed integrals over its pieces
items.strategy: Choose the finite break partition from the hypothesis. Apply the $C^1$ formula to every restriction using its one-sided endpoint derivative extensions, then add the lengths with subdivision additivity. Corners are allowed because no equality of derivatives across a break is asserted.

items.title: The arc-length function $s_\gamma(t)=L(\gamma|_{[a,t]})$ of a rectifiable path
The arc-length function is continuous and nondecreasing, with increments equal to subpath lengths; it is strictly increasing exactly when no nondegenerate subpath is constant
items.strategy: Additivity gives $s(v)-s(u)=L(\gamma|_{[u,v]})\ge0$. Each coordinate is continuous and BV by the componentwise theorem; the published jump theorem makes each scalar variation function continuous. Bound each subpath length by the sum of its coordinate variations to squeeze the increment of $s$ to zero from either side, including endpoints. Finally use the chord bound on every pair of points in a subinterval to show that its length is zero exactly when the path is constant there, giving the strictness criterion.

items.title: Every rectifiable path factors through its arc-length function as a unit-speed path on $[0,L]$
items.strategy: Continuity makes the nondecreasing length function onto $[0,L]$. Define the new path by $\bar\gamma(s(t))=\gamma(t)$; if two parameters have the same length value, additivity forces the intervening subpath to have zero length and hence equal endpoints, so this is well defined. Apply the named chord bound to each subpath to make $\bar\gamma$ $1$-Lipschitz. Use monotone reparametrization and additivity on arbitrary subintervals of $[0,L]$ to prove their lengths equal their parameter differences. Handle $L=0$ as a singleton-domain constant path.

items.title: A regular $C^1$ path has a $C^1$ arc-length reparametrization with derivative of Euclidean norm one
items.strategy: The $C^1$ length formula gives $s(t)=\int_a^t\lVert\gamma'\rVert$ and the pointwise FTC gives $s'=\lVert\gamma'\rVert>0$. Thus $s$ is a strictly increasing continuous bijection. Apply the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem and the chain rule to $\bar\gamma=\gamma\circ s^{-1}$; division by the speed gives derivative norm one. Compactness and positivity make the inverse derivative continuous, including its one-sided endpoint extensions.

pages.title: Arc Length and Rectifiable Curves: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A line segment has length equal to the distance between its endpoints, and a finitely piecewise-linear path has length equal to the sum of its edge lengths
items.strategy: For a line segment every ordered chord is a nonnegative scalar multiple of the same displacement vector, so every polygonal sum telescopes to the endpoint distance. Apply the piecewise-$C^1$ formula or subdivision additivity to a finite vertex list, retaining zero-length edges and repeated vertices.

items.title: For every $\theta\ge0$, the unit-circle path $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,\theta]$ has length $\theta$
items.strategy: Differentiate componentwise and use the Pythagorean identity to make the Euclidean speed identically one. The C1 speed formula and the integral of the constant function one give length $\theta$; when $\theta=0$, use the singleton-interval convention directly. This is the arc-length computation that identifies the trigonometric parameter as radian measure.

items.title: The continuous path $\gamma(x)=(x,x\sin(1/x))$ on $[0,1]$, with $\gamma(0)=(0,0)$, is not rectifiable
items.strategy: For $m\ge0$ put $x_m=2/((2m+1)\pi)$. Positivity of $\pi$, the reciprocal Archimedean estimate, and the quarter-turn shift formulas show that $x_m\downarrow0$ and $x_m\sin(1/x_m)=(-1)^m x_m$; discard a finite initial segment so every retained $x_m$ lies in $(0,1]$. Successive vertical increments are then $x_m+x_{m+1}\ge 1/(\pi(m+1))$. The A-page $p$-series theorem specialized at $p=1$, together with the nonnegative-partial-sum criterion, makes these tail variation sums unbounded. Partitions containing reversed finite retained segments thus show that the second coordinate is not BV, and the componentwise rectifiability theorem makes the path nonrectifiable.

items.title: $\gamma(t)=(t,|t|)$ on $[-1,1]$ is rectifiable of length $2\sqrt{2}$ but is not differentiable at $0$
items.strategy: Split at zero. Each restriction is affine with constant speed $\sqrt2$, so the piecewise-$C^1$ formula gives two contributions of $\sqrt2$. The left and right difference quotients at zero are $(1,-1)$ and $(1,1)$, so the vector derivative does not exist there.

items.title: Two paths can have the same trace and endpoints but different lengths: one traverses $[0,1]$ once and another traverses it forward, backward, and forward
items.strategy: Use the identity path on $[0,1]$ and a three-piece affine path taking the successive values $0,1,0,1$. Both have trace $[0,1]$ and endpoints $0,1$. The polygonal-path formula gives lengths one and three, showing that length belongs to the parametrized path rather than its point set.

items.title: Sawtooth paths converge uniformly to a line segment while every sawtooth has length $\sqrt2$ and the limit has length $1$
items.strategy: On the uniform $n$-partition of $[0,1]$, join successive points whose horizontal separation is $1/n$ and whose vertical coordinates alternate between $0$ and $1/n$. The vertical sup norm is at most $1/n$, so the paths converge uniformly to $(t,0)$. Each of the $n$ affine edges has length $\sqrt2/n$, while the limit segment has length one.

items.title: The graph path $t\mapsto(t,c(t))$ of the Cantor function is rectifiable although its second coordinate is not absolutely continuous
items.strategy: The Cantor function is continuous and nondecreasing with endpoint values zero and one. The A-page Jordan-decomposition theorem, specialized as $c=c-0$, makes it BV; the identity coordinate is BV directly, and componentwise continuity makes the graph a path. The componentwise BV theorem then makes the graph rectifiable and bounds its length between its endpoint chord and two. To prove the second coordinate is not absolutely continuous without citing the published example, derive from the Cantor-set recursion and ternary/binary definition that the $2^n$ surviving stage intervals have total length $(2/3)^n$ and Cantor endpoint increments $2^{-n}$ each. The geometric-null lemma makes the total lengths arbitrarily small while the sum of image increments stays one, contradicting the A-page definition of absolute continuity.

pages.title: Formal Power Series

items.title: Formal power series over a commutative ring and the coefficient-extraction functional $[x^n]$
items.strategy: For a commutative ring $R$, define $R[[x]]$ as all coefficient functions $a:\mathbb N	o R$, with coefficientwise addition and Cauchy product $[x^n](fg)=\sum_{i+j=n}[x^i]f[x^j]g$. Define $x$ as the sequence supported at $1$, constants at $0$, and $[x^n]$ as evaluation at $n$. State once, prominently, that $x$ is an indeterminate and that no analytic convergence is asserted. Identify $R[x]$ with the finitely supported series, but leave the homomorphism proof to the next item.

items.title: Cauchy multiplication makes $R[[x]]$ a commutative ring containing $R[x]$ as the finitely supported subring
items.strategy: Check the ring laws coefficientwise. Each coefficient uses only a finite triangle of indices; associativity is finite Fubini over triples $i+j+k=n$, and distributivity is splitting a finite sum. Show constants and finitely supported coefficient sequences are closed, and that the inclusion $R[x]\hookrightarrow R[[x]]$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism agreeing coefficient-for-coefficient with the published polynomial convolution.

items.title: Coefficient extraction is $R$-linear, separates formal series, shifts under multiplication by $x^k$, and converts products to finite convolution
items.strategy: Read every clause directly from coefficient functions: $[x^n](f+g)$ and $[x^n](rf)$ are pointwise, equality of all coefficients is equality of functions, $[x^n](x^kf)$ is $[x^{n-k}]f$ for $n\ge k$ and $0$ otherwise, and the product clause is the defining finite convolution. Include $n=0$ and $k>n$ explicitly.

items.title: Order of a formal series, congruence modulo $x^N$, and the $x$-adic notions of convergence and Cauchy sequence
items.strategy: For nonzero $f$, define $\operatorname{ord}_x(f)$ as its least nonzero coefficient index and set $\operatorname{ord}_x(0)=+\infty$. Define $f\equiv g\pmod{x^N}$ by equality through degree $N-1$, equivalently $\operatorname{ord}_x(f-g)\ge N$. A sequence converges when every finite coefficient prefix eventually stabilises, and is Cauchy when every prefix eventually agrees pairwise. This algebraic topology has no metric or analytic convergence dependency.

items.title: Formal order is non-Archimedean under sums and additive under products over a domain
items.strategy: Show $\operatorname{ord}_x(f+g)\ge\min(\operatorname{ord}_x f,\operatorname{ord}_x g)$ and identify the leading coefficient when the two orders differ or do not cancel. For products over an arbitrary commutative ring prove the lower bound; if the product of the two leading coefficients is nonzero, equality holds. Specialise to an integral domain to obtain exact additivity and no zero divisors in $R[[x]]$. Treat zero through the declared $+\infty$ conventions rather than cancelling it.

items.title: Summable families of formal series are locally finite in every coefficient range
items.strategy: For a family $(f_i)_{i\in I}$, require that for every $N$ only finitely many indices have a nonzero coefficient below $N$. Define its sum coefficientwise by the resulting finite sum. For a sequence $(u_k)$ with $\operatorname{ord}_x(u_k)\to+\infty$, define $\prod_k(1+u_k)$ by eventual stabilisation modulo every $x^N$. Include the empty family and empty product.

items.title: Summable formal families may be regrouped and rearranged, distribute over multiplication, and have well-defined locally finite products
items.strategy: Work modulo $x^N$, where only finitely many family members and finitely many coefficients survive. Apply finite reindexing and Fubini there, then use coefficient extensionality for the unrestricted identities. For products, show the partial products are eventually constant modulo each $x^N$ and are unchanged by permutations or finite regrouping. State hypotheses separately for sums and products so no analytic absolute-convergence language appears.

items.title: $R[[x]]$ is complete in the $x$-adic topology and $R[x]$ is dense by truncation
items.strategy: Given a Cauchy sequence, define coefficient $n$ of the limit to be the eventual value of coefficient $n$; the Cauchy condition makes that value defined and gives convergence. Uniqueness follows by coefficient separation. Conversely, the truncations $\sum_{n<N}[x^n]f\,x^n$ are polynomials and agree with $f$ modulo $x^N$. Explicitly include the zero ring and the constant-series case.

items.title: A formal power series is a unit exactly when its constant coefficient is a unit
items.strategy: If $fg=1$, the constant-coefficient equation makes $[x^0]f$ a unit. Conversely, if $a_0=[x^0]f$ has inverse, define $b_0=a_0^{-1}$ and recursively $b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{1\le i\le n}a_i b_{n-i}$. Verify each product coefficient is $1$ at $0$ and $0$ thereafter. The recursion is in the coefficient ring and works for every commutative ring, including the zero ring.

items.title: For a field $K$, $K[[x]]$ is a domain and its nonunits form the unique maximal ideal $xK[[x]]$
items.strategy: Use exact order additivity to prove the domain claim. The unit criterion says precisely that nonunits have zero constant term, and the shift formula identifies those series with $xK[[x]]$. This is a proper ideal; any ideal strictly containing it contains a series with nonzero constant coefficient, hence a unit, hence the whole ring. Any maximal ideal contains no unit and therefore lies in $xK[[x]]$, proving uniqueness. Check the constant and zero-series boundaries.

items.title: Composition $f\circ g$ of formal series when the outer series is a polynomial or the inner series has zero constant term
items.strategy: Define $f\circ g=\sum_{n\ge0}[x^n]f\,g^n$. If $f$ is a polynomial this is finite. Otherwise require $[x^0]g=0$, so $\operatorname{ord}_x(g^n)\ge n$ and the family is summable. State that unrestricted composition at a nonzero constant is not defined over a bare ring because one coefficient could require an infinite sum.

items.title: Admissible formal composition is associative and substitution by a zero-constant series is a ring homomorphism
items.strategy: For $g(0)=0$, prove $(f+h)\circ g=f\circ g+h\circ g$, $(fh)\circ g=(f\circ g)(h\circ g)$, $1\circ g=1$, and associativity whenever all displayed compositions are admissible. Reduce every coefficient to finite sums and use the summable-family rearrangement theorem. Record $x\circ f=f$ and $f\circ x=f$, and do not assert commutativity of composition.

items.title: A zero-constant formal series has a compositional inverse exactly when its linear coefficient is a unit
items.strategy: Necessity comes from the coefficient of $x$ in $f\circ g=x$. For sufficiency, write $f=a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots$ and recursively choose coefficient $b_n$ of $g$ so that $[x^n](f\circ g)$ is $0$ for $n>1$; the unknown occurs only as $a_1b_n$. This constructs a unique left inverse. Associativity then shows it is also the unique right inverse. Include the zero ring and the impossible zero linear coefficient when $1\ne0$.

items.title: The formal derivative $D(\sum a_nx^n)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$
items.strategy: Define multiplication by the natural number $n$ as repeated addition in the coefficient ring, so the definition works in every characteristic. Define iterated derivatives and note, without analytic language, that $D(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$ and that $D(x^p)=0$ may occur in characteristic $p$.

items.title: Formal differentiation is linear and satisfies product, power, quotient, chain, and coefficient-recovery laws
items.strategy: Compare coefficients for linearity and the product rule, then induct for powers and differentiate $ff^{-1}=1$ for the quotient rule. Prove the chain rule first for monomials and extend through summable families under the composition hypotheses. Over a commutative ring containing the rationals, show $[x^n]f=D^nf(0)/n!$; over arbitrary characteristic state the Hasse-derivative replacement rather than dividing by a possibly nonunit factorial. Absorb the formal l'Hopital-at-zero identity for a denominator of order one as a final clause.

items.title: Formal exponential, logarithm, and binomial powers over a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
items.strategy: Define a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra here as a commutative ring $R$ equipped with a unital ring homomorphism $\mathbb Q\to R$. For $u\in xR[[x]]$, define $\exp(u)=\sum u^n/n!$, $\log(1+u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n-1}u^n/n$, and $(1+u)^c=\exp(c\log(1+u))$ for $c\in R$. Summability follows from $\operatorname{ord}_x(u^n)\ge n$; no analytic exponential or logarithm is invoked.

items.title: Formal $\exp$ and $\log$ are inverse homomorphisms and formal binomial powers obey the expected addition laws
items.strategy: Use finite coefficientwise binomial convolution to prove $\exp(u+v)=\exp(u)\exp(v)$. Differentiate $\log(1+u)$ and use the chain rule to show $\log(\exp u)=u$ and $\exp(\log(1+u))=1+u$, with constant terms fixing the integration constants. Deduce $\log((1+u)(1+v))=\log(1+u)+\log(1+v)$ and $(1+u)^{c+d}=(1+u)^c(1+u)^d$; also identify coefficients with the generalized binomial products $c(c-1)\cdots(c-n+1)/n!$.

items.title: Every $1+u$ with $u\in xR[[x]]$ has a unique $k$th root with constant coefficient $1$ in a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
items.strategy: Take $(1+u)^{1/k}$ from the formal power construction and use the exponent law for existence. If $v^k=1+u$ and $v(0)=1$, then $\log(v^k)=k\log v=\log(1+u)$; multiply by $1/k$ and apply $\exp$ for uniqueness. State $k\ge1$ explicitly and isolate $u=0$.

items.title: Formal Laurent series $K((x))$, their order, derivative, and residue
items.strategy: For a field $K$, define $K((x))$ as coefficient functions on $\mathbb Z$ with support bounded below, with finite convolution. Define order as the least occupied exponent, formal derivative termwise for all integer exponents, and $\operatorname{res}(f)=[x^{-1}]f$. Cite the published real construction for conventions and make clear that this item generalises coefficients while changing the indeterminate from $t^{-1}$ to $x$.

items.title: Formal residues satisfy integration by parts, logarithmic differentiation, and change of variables
items.strategy: First show $\operatorname{res}(Df)=0$ directly. The product rule gives $\operatorname{res}((Df)g)=-\operatorname{res}(fDg)$. Factor a nonzero Laurent series as $x^m$ times a unit to obtain $\operatorname{res}(Df/f)=m$. When $K$ contains $\mathbb Q$, for $g\in xK[[x]]$ with nonzero linear term prove $\operatorname{res}(f(g)Dg)=\operatorname{res}(f)$ by checking Laurent monomials, including the exceptional exponent $-1$ separately; the characteristic-zero hypothesis licenses division by $m+1$ away from that exponent.

items.title: Lagrange–Bürmann inversion extracts coefficients of a compositional inverse and of functions of it
items.strategy: Let $K$ be a field containing $\mathbb Q$, let $w=x\phi(w)$ with $\phi(0)\ne0$, and let $H\in K[[x]]$. For $n\ge1$, prove $[x^n]H(w)=\frac1n[u^{n-1}]H'(u)\phi(u)^n$ by writing coefficient extraction as a residue, substituting the inverse relation, and applying residue integration by parts and change of variables. Derive $[x^n]w^k=\frac{k}{n}[u^{n-k}]\phi(u)^n$ for $1\le k\le n$, with coefficient $0$ for $k>n$. This is a proof in scope, not an external fallback.

items.title: $K[[x]]$ embeds in $K((x))$ as the nonnegative-order subring; every nonzero Laurent series is uniquely $x^{v(h)}u$ with $u\in K[[x]]^\times$ and inverse $x^{-v(h)}u^{-1}$
items.strategy: Embed $K[[x]]$ by extending coefficients to vanish at negative indices and identify its image by nonnegative order. For nonzero $h\in K((x))$, shift by its Laurent order $v(h)$ to obtain a unique $u\in K[[x]]$ with nonzero constant coefficient; apply the unit criterion and verify directly that $h^{-1}=x^{-v(h)}u^{-1}$. For $K=\mathbb R$, send $x^n$ to $t^{-n}$ and check coefficients, convolution, order, units, and inverses against the published real Laurent items. Do not invoke a field-of-fractions or localisation construction.

pages.title: Formal Power Series — Examples

items.title: The formal geometric identity $(1-x)^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ holds over every commutative ring
items.strategy: Multiply coefficientwise: the constant coefficient is $1$ and every positive coefficient is $1-1=0$. Emphasise that this is local finiteness of the Cauchy product, not convergence of numerical partial sums.

items.title: Negative binomial series: $(1-x)^{-m}=\sum_{n\ge0}\binom{m+n-1}{n}x^n$ for $m\ge1$
items.strategy: Raise the formal geometric series to the $m$th power and count weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts, or equivalently specialise the formal binomial-power coefficient formula. Check $m=1$ and $n=0$ explicitly.

items.title: The constant-one square root of $1-4x$ and its first coefficients
items.strategy: Apply the unique-root corollary over $\mathbb Q$, expand the generalized binomial coefficients through degree $5$, and square the truncation modulo $x^6$ as an independent check. Keep this algebraic; do not discuss branches or radii of convergence.

items.title: Lagrange inversion gives the Catalan coefficients of the inverse of $x-x^2$
items.strategy: Write the inverse $w$ as $w=x/(1-w)$ and apply Lagrange inversion with $\phi(u)=(1-u)^{-1}$. Obtain $[x^n]w=\frac1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$, list the first six coefficients, and verify $w-w^2=x$ through that degree.

items.title: The compositional inverse of $x/(1-x)$ is $x/(1+x)$
items.strategy: Use the two formal geometric identities to compose in both orders and simplify to $x$. Then display the alternating coefficient recursion from the general inverse construction.

items.title: $x$ has no multiplicative inverse in $R[[x]]$ although it is invertible in $K((x))$ when $R=K$ is a field
items.strategy: The constant coefficient of $xg$ is always $0$, so it cannot equal $1$ in a nonzero ring. In the Laurent field the monomial $x^{-1}$ exists and multiplies $x$ to $1$. This separates power-series units from Laurent-field units.

items.title: Substituting $1$ into $1+x+x^2+\cdots$ is not a defined formal composition
items.strategy: The putative constant coefficient would be an infinite sum of copies of $1_R$, which the ring operations do not define. Contrast with substitution of $x^2$, where each coefficient has at most one contributor. This tests the zero-constant hypothesis exactly.

items.title: An infinite family of constant series $1$ is not summable in the formal topology
items.strategy: At coefficient $0$ infinitely many family members are nonzero, violating local finiteness already modulo $x$. Contrast with the family $(x^n)_{n\ge0}$, which is summable and yields the geometric series.

items.title: Nonzero constant series can multiply to zero in $(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)[[x]]$
items.strategy: Regard the nonzero residue class $2$ as a constant series. Its square is the zero series because $2\cdot2=0$ modulo $4$. This verifies why product-order additivity and the domain conclusion require a domain coefficient ring.

items.title: Intervals in a poset; locally finite, lower-finite and upper-finite posets
items.strategy: Define $[x,y]=\{z:x\le z\le y\}$. Locally finite means every such interval is finite; lower-finite and upper-finite mean every principal ideal and principal filter is finite. State that either one-sided condition implies local finiteness.

items.title: The incidence functions $I(P,R)$ of a locally finite poset and their convolution
items.strategy: For a locally finite poset $P$ and commutative ring $R$, define functions on comparable pairs and $(f*g)(x,y)=\sum_{x\le z\le y}f(x,z)g(z,y)$. Local finiteness and the general finite-sum definition make the operation well defined.

items.title: The delta and zeta incidence functions
items.strategy: Define $\delta(x,y)=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\zeta(x,y)=1$ on every comparable pair.

items.title: Incidence convolution is associative and distributes over pointwise addition
items.strategy: Expand both bracketings as the same finite sum over pairs $x\le u\le v\le y$, using finite Fubini and bijective reindexing. Prove both distributive laws termwise.

items.title: Pointwise addition and convolution make $I(P,R)$ a ring with identity $\delta$
items.strategy: Obtain the pointwise additive abelian group from the function-ring construction, use the preceding lemma for multiplication and distributivity, and compute $\delta*f=f=f*\delta$.

items.title: If every diagonal value of an incidence function is a unit, recursive interval formulas construct both a left and a right convolution inverse
items.strategy: Use strong induction on the finite cardinality of $[x,y]$. Solve the equations $(f*g)(x,y)=0$ and $(h*f)(x,y)=0$ off the diagonal after isolating the diagonal unit. Then $h=h*(f*g)=(h*f)*g=g$, so the one-sided inverses coincide.

items.title: An incidence function is convolution-invertible if and only if every diagonal value is a unit
items.strategy: Necessity follows by evaluating an inverse equation on $(x,x)$. Sufficiency is the recursive construction. State the criterion for arbitrary locally finite $P$, including infinite $P$.

items.title: The integer-valued Möbius function $\mu_P$ of a locally finite poset
items.strategy: Take the inverse of the zeta function in $I(P,\mathbb Z)$. Existence and uniqueness come from the invertibility criterion because every diagonal value is $1$. This fixes the coefficient ring as $\mathbb Z$ and avoids a characteristic-dependent second notion.

items.title: The Möbius recurrence: $\mu_P(x,x)=1$ and both interval sums of $\mu_P$ vanish when $x<y$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\mu*\zeta=\delta$ and $\zeta*\mu=\delta$. Isolate the endpoint term to obtain the two recursive formulas and uniqueness.

items.title: Möbius inversion on a lower-finite poset, with the dual upper-finite form
items.strategy: For functions $f,g:P\to R$ into a commutative ring, prove $g(y)=\sum_{x\le y}f(x)$ iff $f(y)=\sum_{x\le y}\mu_P(x,y)g(x)$. Interchange the finite double sum and use the recurrence. State and prove the order-dual upper-finite form separately.

items.title: Both forms of Möbius inversion hold on every finite poset
items.strategy: Every principal ideal and filter is a subset of the finite ground set, hence finite; apply both halves of the preceding theorem.

items.title: The Möbius function of a product poset is the product of the Möbius functions
items.strategy: Show intervals in $P\times Q$ are Cartesian products of intervals and hence finite. Verify that the proposed product satisfies the Möbius recurrence using finite Fubini.

items.title: For $A\subseteq B$ in a finite Boolean lattice, $\mu(A,B)=(-1)^{\lvert B\setminus A\rvert}$
items.strategy: Identify the interval $[A,B]$ with a product of two-element chains indexed by $B\setminus A$, then apply the product theorem. Alternatively verify the recurrence by the alternating binomial sum; keep one route as the proof and the other as a Remark.

items.title: The complementary inclusion-exclusion formula is Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
items.strategy: Index intersections by subsets of the sieve index set, apply finite-poset Möbius inversion, insert the Boolean-lattice formula, and match every term and sign to the published complementary sieve identity.

items.title: On a finite chain, the Möbius function is $1$ on the diagonal, $-1$ on covers and $0$ on longer intervals
items.strategy: Induct on interval cardinality using the recurrence. The first nontrivial interval gives $-1$ and every longer interval has partial sum $1-1=0$ before the final term.

items.title: The divisibility poset of positive integers
items.strategy: Restrict integer divisibility to positive integers and verify reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity. Its interval $[a,b]$ consists of the positive integers $d$ with $a\mid d\mid b$.

items.title: The divisibility poset is lower-finite, and each divisor interval factorises as a product of finite chains of prime exponents
items.strategy: Positive divisors of $n$ lie in a finite initial segment. Use canonical prime factorisation and valuations to biject divisors with exponent tuples $0\le e_i\le v_{p_i}(n)$, preserving and reflecting divisibility.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function $\mu(n)$ from prime factorisation
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$, set $\mu(n)=0$ when some prime square divides $n$, and $\mu(n)=(-1)^r$ when $n$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes. Use uniqueness of prime factorisation to prove $r$ and the value are well defined, including $\mu(1)=1$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is the poset Möbius function of divisibility: $\mu(n)=\mu_{\mid}(1,n)$
items.strategy: Use the prime-exponent product decomposition of the divisor interval, the product theorem and the finite-chain formula. A repeated prime exponent contributes zero; otherwise every nontrivial chain contributes $-1$.

items.title: Classical Möbius inversion over positive divisors
items.strategy: Apply lower-finite poset inversion to the divisibility order and substitute the agreement theorem. Give both standard equivalent indexings, with $\mu(d)$ and with $\mu(n/d)$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is multiplicative on coprime positive integers
items.strategy: For coprime $m,n$, divisors of $mn$ split uniquely into a divisor of $m$ and a divisor of $n$ by prime factorisation. Apply the product-poset theorem and the agreement theorem.

items.title: False: convolution defines an incidence algebra for every poset
items.strategy: Refute with the companion's poset having an infinite interval: convolution of the constant-one functions asks for an infinite sum not defined by the ring axioms.

items.title: False: $\mu_P(x,y)$ depends only on the cardinality of $[x,y]$
items.strategy: Compare a four-element chain, whose endpoint value is $0$, with the four-element diamond, whose endpoint value is $1$.

items.title: False: classical Möbius inversion and inclusion-exclusion are unrelated inversion principles
items.strategy: Refute by citing their common finite-poset inversion theorem and the two dictionary results for the divisibility and Boolean posets.

pages.title: Incidence Algebras and Möbius Inversion — Examples

items.title: The full Möbius table of the Boolean lattice $2^{[3]}$
items.strategy: List comparable pairs by rank difference and assign $1,-1,1,-1$ according to the Boolean-lattice formula, checking representative recurrence sums.

items.title: The Möbius table of a four-element chain
items.strategy: Compute recursively: diagonal entries are $1$, cover entries are $-1$, and all entries spanning at least two covers are $0$.

items.title: The Möbius function on the divisor poset of $12$ and its agreement with $\mu(1),\mu(2),\mu(3),\mu(4),\mu(6),\mu(12)$
items.strategy: Draw the divisor order, compute from the recurrence, and compare each value with the prime-factor definition.

items.title: The endpoint Möbius value of the four-element diamond is $1$
items.strategy: Compute the two cover values as $-1$, then solve $1-1-1+\mu(\bot,\top)=0$.

items.title: Möbius inversion of $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$ gives $\varphi(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)(n/d)$
items.strategy: Apply classical Möbius inversion to the totient divisor-sum theorem and verify the formula numerically at $n=12$.

items.title: A poset with a bottom, a top and countably many incomparable middle elements has an infinite interval, so convolution of constant-one functions is not defined
items.strategy: Use the tagged set $\{\bot,\top\}\cup(\mathbb N\times\{m\})$, with every middle element strictly between the endpoints. The endpoint convolution sum has one term for each middle element.

items.title: On a two-element chain, an incidence function with a zero diagonal value is not convolution-invertible
items.strategy: Set $f(0,0)=0$ and evaluate any purported inverse equation on $(0,0)$; the diagonal product remains zero rather than one.

items.title: A four-element chain and a four-element diamond have equal-size endpoint intervals but Möbius values $0$ and $1$
items.strategy: Place the two preceding computations side by side and identify the different internal order structures that change the recurrence.

The finite uniform Ramsey theorem follows a second time from the infinite theorem by a finitely branching tree of bad finite colourings
Canonical Ramsey theorem for pairs: on an infinite subset a colouring is constant, injective, left-dependent, or right-dependent
Finite colour focussing extends equally coloured progressions to a longer monochromatic arithmetic progression
Van der Waerden's theorem, strengthened so the progression and its common difference have one colour
The van der Waerden number $W(k,c)$ as the least interval length forcing a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression
Schur's theorem: every finite colouring of a sufficiently long positive initial interval $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has positive monochromatic $x,y,z$ with $x+y=z$
The Schur number $S(c)$ as the largest $N$ for which $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has a $c$-colouring with no positive monochromatic solution of $x+y=z$

pages.title: Extremal Graph Theory

items.title: Ordinary-subgraph extremal number $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$, Turán graph $T_{n,r}$, and balanced blowup $H[s]$
items.strategy: Fix ordinary, not induced, subgraph containment. For a forbidden graph $H$ with at least one edge, define $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$ as the maximum edge count of an $n$-vertex graph containing no ordinary copy of $H$; the edgeless $n$-vertex graph makes the finite candidate set nonempty. Define $T_{n,r}$ as the complete $r$-partite graph whose part sizes differ by at most one, allowing empty parts when $r>n$. Define $H[s]$ by replacing every vertex of $H$ with an independent $s$-set and every edge with all cross edges. State the induced-free terminology disagreement in a convention remark and never use bare '$H$-free' ambiguously.

items.title: The exact edge count of $T_{n,r}$ and the unique balancing maximum among complete $r$-partite graphs
items.strategy: If $n=qr+a$ with $0\le a<r$, count missing within-part pairs to obtain $e(T_{n,r})=\binom n2-(r-a)\binom q2-a\binom{q+1}2$. Moving one vertex from a part at least two larger than another increases the edge count; iterate to balance. Equality forces all nonempty part sizes to differ by at most one, giving uniqueness up to graph isomorphism. Include $n=0$, $r=1$, and $r>n$.

items.title: Mantel's theorem: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K_3)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, uniquely attained by $T_{n,2}$
items.strategy: Give an independent induction, not a reference to Turán. For a triangle-free graph with an edge $uv$, the two open neighbourhoods are disjoint apart from their opposite endpoints, so $\deg u+\deg v\le n$. Delete $u,v$, apply induction to the remaining $n-2$ vertices, and restore exactly $\deg u+\deg v-1$ incident edges. Verify the floor recurrence. Track equality: the smaller graph is balanced complete bipartite and the degree-sum equality forces $u,v$ into opposite parts with every allowed cross edge, yielding $T_{n,2}$. Handle edgeless graphs and $n=0,1,2$ separately.

items.title: Zykov symmetrisation turns an extremal clique-free graph into a complete multipartite graph without losing edges
items.strategy: For nonadjacent vertices $u,v$, replacing the lower-degree vertex by a twin of the higher-degree vertex preserves $K_{r+1}$-avoidance and does not decrease edges. Apply the operation to degree classes with a termination statistic: first maximise edges, then the sum of squares of twin-class sizes. At termination nonadjacency is an equivalence relation, so the graph is complete multipartite. Record the equality case needed later: an edge-maximiser can be symmetrised without changing its edge count, and reversing an equality-preserving step cannot create a second nonisomorphic maximiser once balanced part sizes are forced.

items.title: Turán's theorem with equality: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K_{r+1})=e(T_{n,r})$, and $T_{n,r}$ is the unique extremal graph
items.strategy: Use Zykov symmetrisation to reduce an extremal $K_{r+1}$-avoiding graph to a complete $k$-partite graph with $k\le r$. The balancing lemma shows the largest such edge count is $e(T_{n,r})$ and identifies the balanced parts. For equality, carry the equality conditions through symmetrisation (or present the standard duplication proof directly) to show the original graph was already complete multipartite and balanced. State the exact quotient-remainder formula from the preceding lemma, not just the asymptotic bound. Cover $r=1$, $n=0$, and $r\ge n$.

items.title: Turán graphs give the Ramsey lower bound $R(s,t)\ge(s-1)(t-1)+1$
items.strategy: On $(s-1)(t-1)$ vertices split into $t-1$ classes of size $s-1$, colour within-class pairs red and cross-class pairs blue. Red cliques have size at most $s-1$, while blue cliques use at most one vertex from each of the $t-1$ classes. Thus there is neither a red $s$-set nor a blue $t$-set. Identify the blue graph as $T_{(s-1)(t-1),t-1}$ and translate the witness through the published arrow and Ramsey-number definitions. Check $s,t\ge2$.

items.title: Edge density and the asymptotic notations $O$, $o$, $\Omega$, and $\Theta$ for extremal functions
items.strategy: For an $n$-vertex graph with $n\ge2$, define edge density as $e(G)/\binom n2$. Define $f=O(g)$ and $f=o(g)$ with explicit constants and quantifiers as $n\to\infty$, and define $\Omega,\Theta$ from $O$. Fix that all forbidden graphs and integer parameters are held constant in asymptotic statements. Avoid defining density for $n<2$, where the denominator vanishes.

items.title: $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)/\binom n2$ is nonincreasing for $n\ge2$
items.strategy: For a fixed forbidden graph $H$ with at least one edge, take an extremal $(n+1)$-vertex graph and double-count pairs $(v,e)$ where edge $e$ remains after deleting vertex $v$. Every $n$-vertex induced subgraph contains no ordinary copy of $H$, so its edges are at most $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$. Simplify the resulting natural-number inequality before dividing by positive binomial coefficients. State $n\ge2$.

items.title: Every finite graph with an edge has a Turán density $\pi(H)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{ex}(n,H)/\binom n2$
items.strategy: The normalized sequence is nonincreasing and lies in $[0,1]$, hence has an infimum and converges to it. Define that limit to be $\pi(H)$. Give the equivalent epsilon-threshold formulation used by supersaturation. Keep the standing hypothesis that $H$ has at least one edge, so the extremal candidate family is never empty.

items.title: Above Turán density, a graph contains a positive-density family of copies of the forbidden graph
items.strategy: For a fixed graph $H$ with at least one edge and $\varepsilon>0$, choose a fixed sample size $m$ at which the extremal density is below $\pi(H)+\varepsilon/2$. In an $n$-vertex graph of density at least $\pi(H)+\varepsilon$, average edges over all $m$-vertex subsets to show a positive fraction are above threshold and contain $H$. Double-count each unlabelled copy across the $m$-sets containing it to obtain $\delta n^{v(H)}$ copies. Track constants and $n\ge n_0$ explicitly.

items.title: The Zarankiewicz number $z(m,n;s,t)$ for a forbidden $K_{s,t}$ in a bipartite graph
items.strategy: For fixed disjoint sides $A,B$ of sizes $m,n$, define $z(m,n;s,t)$ as the maximum number of cross edges with no ordinary $K_{s,t}$ whose $s$-side lies in $A$ and $t$-side in $B$. Record the transpose symmetry $z(m,n;s,t)=z(n,m;t,s)$ and the relation to $\operatorname{ex}(N,K_{s,t})$. Require positive $s,t$; permit empty host sides.

items.title: The Kővári–Sós–Turán common-neighbour count and the discrete convexity lower bound for degree sums
items.strategy: In a bipartite $K_{s,t}$-avoiding graph with sides $A,B$, count pairs $(S,b)$ with $S\in[A]^s$ and $S\subseteq N(b)$. The upper count is $(t-1)\binom{|A|}{s}$ and the lower expression is $\sum_{b\in B}\binom{\deg b}{s}$. Prove the needed lower bound at a fixed total degree by smoothing integer degrees: moving one unit from a value at least two larger to the smaller value cannot increase the sum. This avoids citing real Jensen and includes average degree below $s-1$.

items.title: Kővári–Sós–Turán: exact bipartite and ordinary-graph upper bounds for excluding $K_{s,t}$
items.strategy: For positive $s\le t$, combine the common-neighbour bound with the discrete convex estimate to prove $z(m,n;s,t)\le (t-1)^{1/s}m n^{1-1/s}+(s-1)n$ in the stated orientation. Apply the symmetric count directly to an $N$-vertex graph to obtain $\operatorname{ex}(N,K_{s,t})\le\tfrac12(t-1)^{1/s}N^{2-1/s}+\tfrac12(s-1)N$, and hence $O_{s,t}(N^{2-1/s})$. Check $s=1$, $N=0$, and the side-orientation convention.

items.title: Every bipartite graph with at least one edge has Turán density zero
items.strategy: If $H$ has bipartition sizes $s,t$, then $H$ is an ordinary subgraph of $K_{s,t}$, so every graph excluding $H$ also excludes $K_{s,t}$. Apply KST and divide by $\binom n2$ to get a quantity tending to $0$. Exclude the edgeless case explicitly and allow isolated vertices by enlarging the two complete parts as needed.

items.title: $r$-uniform hypergraphs and complete balanced $r$-partite $r$-graphs $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$
items.strategy: Define an $r$-uniform hypergraph as a finite vertex set with edges in $[V]^r$. Define ordinary subhypergraph containment, the extremal number, and $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$ on $r$ disjoint $s$-sets with every transversal an edge. State the graph case $r=2$ as a dictionary, and require $r\ge2$, $s\ge1$ for subsequent use.

items.title: Hypergraph KST: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s})=O_{r,s}(n^{r-1/s^{r-1}})=o(n^r)$
items.strategy: Induct on $r$. The base $r=2$ is KST. For the inductive step count copies of $K^{(r)}_{s,1,\ldots,1}$ in two ways: fixing the $s$-set leaves an $(r-1)$-uniform link hypergraph excluding $K^{(r-1)}_{s,\ldots,s}$, while fixing an $(r-1)$-tuple contributes a binomial coefficient of its codegree. Use the same smoothing inequality to compare the lower count with the average codegree. Solve the exponent recurrence and state only the little-$o$ consequence where it is used by Erdős–Stone.

items.title: Every finite graph $H$ with $\chi(H)=r$ is an ordinary subgraph of $K_r[s]$ for some $s$
items.strategy: Take a proper $r$-colouring, let $s$ be the largest colour-class size, inject each colour class into one of the $s$-vertex blowup parts, and observe that every edge joins different colours and therefore maps to a cross edge. Handle $H$ null separately, and for nonnull $H$ use the published existence and boundary convention for $\chi(H)$.

items.title: Erdős–Stone for balanced blowups: $\pi(K_r[s])=1-1/(r-1)$ for $r\ge2$
items.strategy: The lower bound is the $(r-1)$-partite Turán graph. For the upper bound, a graph with density above $\pi(K_r)+\varepsilon$ contains $\delta n^r$ copies of $K_r$ by supersaturation. Form the $r$-uniform hypergraph whose edges are those $r$-cliques. Hypergraph KST forces a $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$, whose supporting graph is $K_r[s]$. Convert the epsilon statement to the density formula and keep $s=1$ as the Turán theorem boundary.

items.title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits: $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)=(1-1/(\chi(H)-1)+o(1))\binom n2$ for every graph with an edge
items.strategy: Let $r=\chi(H)\ge2$. The graph $T_{n,r-1}$ contains no $H$, giving the lower bound. Embed $H$ into a balanced blowup $K_r[s]$; excluding $H$ implies excluding that blowup, so Erdős–Stone gives the matching upper bound. State the equivalent epsilon form with an explicit $n_0(H,\varepsilon)$ and treat bipartite $r=2$ consistently as density $0$. The edgeless graph is excluded from the theorem statement.

items.title: The asymptotic extremal density is determined exactly by chromatic number: $\pi(H)=1-1/(\chi(H)-1)$
items.strategy: Divide the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits asymptotic by $\binom n2$ and use existence of Turán density. Spell out the dichotomy: positive density exactly when $\chi(H)\ge3$, while every bipartite graph with an edge has density $0$, agreeing with KST. This is the short citable chromatic-number formulation required downstream.

items.title: $T_{10,3}=K_{3,3,4}$ has $33$ edges and is the unique $10$-vertex $K_4$-extremal graph
items.strategy: Use $10=3\cdot3+1$ in the exact edge formula, also count the three cross products $3\cdot3+3\cdot4+3\cdot4=33$, and invoke the equality statement of Turán's theorem. Display a $K_4$ obstruction by the three parts.

items.title: $K_{3,4}$ realises $\operatorname{ex}(7,K_3)=12$
items.strategy: Count $3\cdot4=12=\lfloor49/4\rfloor$, note that a bipartite graph contains no triangle, and apply Mantel's exact equality characterization.

items.title: Deleting one edge from $K_{3,4}$ gives a triangle-free graph one edge below the Mantel threshold
items.strategy: Delete a displayed cross edge, recount $11$ edges, and verify triangle-freeness survives. Compare with the unique $12$-edge equality case to distinguish exact extremality from near-extremality without claiming a stability theorem.

items.title: A Turán-partition colouring witnesses $R(4,3)\ge7$
items.strategy: Partition six vertices into three pairs, colour within pairs blue and cross pairs red. A red clique uses at most one vertex per pair, so has size at most $3$; a blue clique lies within one pair, so has size at most $2$. Translate this explicit colouring to failure of $6\to(4,3)^2$.

items.title: The five-cycle is $K_{2,2}$-avoiding and shows the KST problem is not just a complete-bipartite construction
items.strategy: List the five cycle edges and observe that any two vertices have at most one common neighbour, whereas a $K_{2,2}$ would give two. Record its edge count and compare it with the KST upper bound at $N=5$ without asserting the bound is sharp there.

items.title: Every triangle-free graph is bipartite
items.strategy: Instantiate the published cycle definition at $n=5$ and inspect its five edges to show that $C_5$ has no triangle. The published odd-cycle characterisation of bipartite graphs then shows that $C_5$ is not bipartite. This separates Mantel's equality classification from the much weaker hypothesis of triangle-freeness without depending on the neighbouring AI-generated example.

items.title: The Petersen graph has chromatic number $3$, so its Turán density is $1/2$
items.strategy: Use the published two-subset model to exhibit an odd $5$-cycle, ruling out two colours, and give an explicit three-colouring of all ten vertices. Apply the chromatic-density corollary to obtain $1-1/(3-1)=1/2$.

items.title: Every odd cycle $C_{2k+1}$ has Turán density $1/2$
items.strategy: For $k\ge1$, alternate two colours around the cycle until the closing edge forces a third colour, proving $\chi(C_{2k+1})=3$. Apply the chromatic-density corollary to obtain $1-1/(3-1)=1/2$, and contrast this with the zero density of bipartite graphs without claiming an exact finite extremal number.

items.title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits determines the extremal number for every graph
items.strategy: Take $H=K_{2,2}$, for which $\chi(H)=2$. Erdős–Stone–Simonovits then gives only $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)=o(n^2)$, while the page's Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem supplies the strictly sharper upper bound $O(n^{3/2})$. Thus the density theorem determines the quadratic leading term but not the finite extremal number or even its order of growth in the bipartite case.

items.title: A linear map $L:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$ in Euclidean coordinates
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$
items.strategy: Expand $h$ in the published standard basis, use linearity to obtain $Lh=\sum_j h_jL(e_j)$, and read off the unique matrix columns. Bound the norm by the finite triangle inequality and $|h_j|\le\|h\|_2$, taking $K=\sum_j\|L(e_j)\|_2$. Check $m=0$ is outside the standing hypotheses and zero maps give $K=0$.

items.title: A convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ contains every line segment between two of its points
Directional derivatives and partial derivatives of a map $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$
The total (Fréchet) derivative $Df(a)$ as the linear first-order approximation with $o(\|h\|_2)$ remainder
The total derivative at a point is unique
items.strategy: If $L$ and $M$ both satisfy the remainder estimate, test along $h=tv$ inside an open ball about the point. Divide by $|t|$ for $t\ne0$ and use an epsilon contradiction to obtain $(L-M)v=0$ for every $v$, including $v=0$ separately.

items.title: Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity
items.strategy: Bound $Df(a)h$ by the Euclidean linear-map lemma and make the normalized remainder at most one on a sufficiently small ball. The triangle inequality gives $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le(K+1)\|h\|_2$, from which epsilon-delta continuity follows; keep the zero-map and zero-increment cases explicit.

items.title: The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case
A total derivative computes every directional derivative, and its matrix is the Jacobian
items.strategy: Restrict the total remainder estimate to $h=tv$. After division by $t$, homogeneity makes the remainder tend to zero and the derivative of $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ equals $Df(a)v$. Specialize to standard basis vectors and invoke the matrix-column representation to identify the Jacobian, preserving the $v=0$ case.

items.title: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ and the unit direction of steepest ascent is the normalized gradient
items.strategy: Use the Jacobian representation in the scalar case to obtain the inner-product formula. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds unit-direction derivatives by the gradient norm, with equality in the normalized gradient direction when the gradient is nonzero; when it is zero, every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Add or scale the two remainder identities and use the norm triangle inequality or absolute homogeneity. Verify that the proposed derivative is linear, and split the scalar-zero case only where division by its absolute value would otherwise occur.

items.title: The chain rule for total derivatives: $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$
items.strategy: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=Ah+r(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)-g(f(a))=Bk+s(k)$. The local linear bound makes $k=O(\|h\|)$, so $s(k)=o(\|k\|)=o(\|h\|)$, while boundedness of $B$ gives $B r(h)=o(\|h\|)$. Treat $k=0$ without forming the normalized outer remainder and verify the composite linear map explicitly.

items.title: Small coordinate-by-coordinate increments stay inside a Euclidean ball and telescope the total increment
items.strategy: For $h\in\mathbb{R}^m$, define $p_j=a+\sum_{k<j}h_ke_k$. The norm of each coordinate prefix is at most $\|h\|_2$, so a small increment keeps every $p_j$ in the chosen ball. The finite telescoping identity expresses $f(a+h)-f(a)$ as the sum of the increments $f(p_{j+1})-f(p_j)$.

items.title: If all partial derivatives exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous at a point, then the map is totally differentiable there with Jacobian derivative
items.strategy: Choose a ball where every partial derivative vector is uniformly close to its value at the base point. Telescope along coordinate segments using the preceding lemma; apply the published vector mean-value inequality to each segment after subtracting the fixed linear term. Sum the errors and compare the coordinate $1$-norm with the Euclidean norm. Verify the Jacobian map is linear before invoking the definition.

items.title: On a convex open set, a uniform bound $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ implies $\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2$
items.strategy: Parametrize the segment from $x$ to $y$ by $\gamma(t)=x+t(y-x)$. Convexity keeps the curve in the domain, the chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))(y-x)$, and the published vector mean-value inequality supplies the endpoint estimate. Treat $x=y$ directly and use no global operator-norm definition.

items.title: A totally differentiable map with zero derivative on a convex open set is constant
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative mean-value inequality with $M=0$ to arbitrary points of the domain. Include the empty-domain case (vacuously constant under the library's definition) and singleton/zero-dimensional exclusions explicitly rather than importing the later connected-open-set theorem.

items.title: Dimension, openness, norm, Jacobian, and the native Euclidean linear-map agreement seam

pages.title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The polynomial map $(x,y)\mapsto(1+x+2y+x^2,\,2x+3y+xy)$ and its Jacobian
items.strategy: Compute all four partial derivatives with the one-variable algebra and power rules. Their continuity makes the continuous-partials theorem applicable, and the resulting Jacobian matrix gives the total derivative at an arbitrary point. Verify one increment expansion directly as a check on the matrix.

items.title: $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ has both partial derivatives at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: Define the value at the origin to be zero. Both coordinate-axis restrictions are identically zero, so both partial derivatives exist and vanish. Along $y=x\ne0$ the function is $1/2$, contradicting continuity at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^4+y^2)$ tends to zero on every line through the origin but not along $y=x^2$
items.strategy: Define the origin value to be zero. Substitute $(x,y)=(ta,tb)$ and separate $b=0$ from $b\ne0$ to show every straight-line restriction tends to zero. Along $(t,t^2)$ the value is $1/2$, so the map is not continuous at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ has every directional derivative at the origin but is not totally differentiable there
items.strategy: Compute the directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ as $a^2b/(a^2+b^2)$ for $v\ne0$ and zero for $v=0$. Exhibit a failure of additivity of this direction map. If a total derivative existed, the directional-derivative theorem would make the map linear, a contradiction.

items.title: The map $y(x^2+y^2)/x$ off the line $x=0$, extended by zero on that line, has every directional derivative zero at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: On every fixed line through the origin the function is quadratic in the line parameter, so the directional difference quotient tends to zero. Along the curved path $x=y^3$ the values tend to one, proving discontinuity and hence failure of total differentiability.

items.title: A locally constant step map on the disconnected open set $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has zero total derivative but is not globally Lipschitz
items.strategy: In the $\mathbb{R}^1$ identification, take value zero on the negative component and one on the positive component. Each point has a neighbourhood on which the map is constant, so its total derivative is zero. The points $-t$ and $t$ have image distance one and domain distance $2t$, which defeats every proposed global Lipschitz constant for small positive $t$.

items.title: $C^k$ maps and multi-index derivative notation in Euclidean space
The Hessian matrix and critical points of a scalar field
A rectangular second difference equals a mixed partial times the side lengths
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable mean value theorem in one coordinate to the difference across the other coordinate, then apply it again to the resulting one-variable function. State the closed-rectangle and interior differentiability hypotheses exactly.

items.title: Peano's mixed-partial theorem from continuity of one mixed partial
items.strategy: Apply the rectangle formula to shrinking rectangles based at the point. Continuity of one mixed partial controls the quotient, while the assumed existence of the reverse iterated derivative along the coordinate line identifies the other iterated limit.

items.title: Young's theorem: total differentiability of the first partials forces equality of mixed partials
items.strategy: Expand the two first-partial functions at the base point with total-derivative remainders and insert those expansions into a symmetric rectangular difference quotient. Cancellation leaves the two mixed coefficients equal.

items.title: Clairaut–Schwarz theorem for continuous second partial derivatives
items.strategy: Continuity of the relevant second partials gives the hypotheses of Peano's theorem (and, alternatively, Young's differentiability hypothesis); specialize to every coordinate pair.

items.title: The Hessian of a $C^2$ scalar field is symmetric
items.strategy: Apply Clairaut–Schwarz to each pair of coordinate indices and translate the equalities into matrix entries.

items.title: Continuous mixed partials of order $k$ are invariant under permutations
items.strategy: Show invariance under one adjacent transposition by applying Clairaut–Schwarz after freezing the other derivatives; decompose every finite permutation into adjacent transpositions and induct over their number.

items.title: Repeated derivatives along a line expand by the multinomial formula
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative chain rule once, then induct on the derivative order. Use symmetry of higher mixed partials to collect ordered coordinate choices into multinomial coefficients.

items.title: The multivariable Taylor polynomial in multi-index notation
Multivariable Taylor formula with a Lagrange remainder along a line segment
items.strategy: Restrict the function to the segment, apply the one-variable Lagrange Taylor formula, and substitute the line-derivative multinomial expansion. Convexity keeps the segment inside the domain; separate zero increment.

items.title: Multivariable Taylor formula with $o(\|h\|^k)$ remainder
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable Peano theorem to the line restriction and use the multinomial line-derivative identity; convert the scalar parameter remainder to the Euclidean increment norm.

items.title: Second-order Taylor expansion $f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\tfrac12h^TH_f(a)h+o(\|h\|^2)$
items.strategy: Specialize the Peano formula to order two and collect the first- and second-order multi-index terms as the gradient inner product and Hessian quadratic form.

items.title: Local and strict local extrema for scalar fields on Euclidean open sets
Fermat's theorem: an interior differentiable local extremum has zero gradient
items.strategy: Restrict to each coordinate line through the point, apply the one-variable Fermat theorem, and identify the resulting partial derivatives as the gradient coordinates.

items.title: Positive definite, negative definite, semidefinite, and indefinite quadratic forms
A definite quadratic form has a uniform signed bound on the Euclidean unit sphere
items.strategy: For $n\ge 1$, prove directly that the Euclidean unit sphere is nonempty, closed, and bounded: use $e_0$ for nonemptiness, continuity of the Euclidean norm for closedness, and the norm equation for boundedness. Heine-Borel then makes the sphere compact. Prove continuity of the fixed quadratic form from its finite coordinate formula, apply the extreme value theorem, and use definiteness to make the attained minimum positive or the attained maximum negative.

items.title: The multivariable second-derivative test by definiteness of the Hessian
items.strategy: At a critical point combine the second-order Taylor expansion with the uniform sphere bound. Positive or negative definiteness dominates the little-o remainder and gives a strict extremum; two directions of opposite quadratic sign give saddle behaviour. Make the semidefinite case explicitly inconclusive.

items.title: The two-variable Hessian determinant test
items.strategy: For the symmetric matrix with entries $A,B,C$, complete the square when $A\ne0$. The determinant sign classifies definiteness or indefiniteness; if the determinant is zero, state that the test gives no conclusion.

items.title: A constrained local extremum annihilates every velocity of a differentiable parametrization
items.strategy: Compose the objective with each differentiable curve in the constraint set through the point. One-variable Fermat and the total-derivative chain rule give $Df(a)\gamma'(0)=0$.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers for a regular graph constraint $y=\psi(x)$
items.strategy: Parametrize the graph by $x\mapsto(x,\psi(x))$. The parametrized necessary condition says the objective gradient is orthogonal to all graph tangent vectors; solve the coordinate equations to obtain $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla(y-\psi(x))$, whose last coordinate is nonzero.

pages.title: Mixed Partials, Taylor, and Extrema in Several Variables: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Peano's function has unequal mixed partials at the origin
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$ off the origin and zero at the origin, compute the two axis first partials and then their derivatives at zero, obtaining opposite values. Also verify continuity at the origin by a quadratic bound.

items.title: Peano's surface has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Use $f(x,y)=(y-3x^2)(y-x^2)$. Substitution on an arbitrary line gives a positive leading even power near zero, with vertical lines separate; along the parabola $y=2x^2$ the values are negative.

items.title: A smooth flat refinement has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Let $\phi(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x\ne0$ and $\phi(0)=0$, and set $F=(y-3\phi(x))(y-\phi(x))$. Exponential domination proves smooth flatness and linewise positivity; the curve $y=2\phi(x)$ gives negative values approaching the origin.

items.title: $x^2+y^2(1-x)^3$ has a unique critical point, a strict local but nonglobal minimum
items.strategy: Solve the two gradient equations to show the origin is the sole critical point. Its Hessian is positive definite, while values with $x>1$ and sufficiently large $|y|$ are negative, so the local minimum is not global.

items.title: The monkey saddle $x^3-3xy^2$ has an indefinite higher-order critical point
items.strategy: Compute the zero gradient and zero Hessian at the origin, then evaluate along three rays to exhibit alternating signs. Conclude directly that the origin is a saddle although the quadratic test is silent.

items.title: A zero Hessian occurs at a strict minimum, a strict maximum, and a saddle
items.strategy: Compare $x^4+y^4$, $-(x^4+y^4)$, and $x^4-y^4$ at the origin. Compute the common zero gradient and Hessian, then classify by signs.

items.title: A second-order Taylor polynomial computed from gradient and Hessian data
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=e^x(1+y+y^2)$ at the origin, compute the value, gradient, and Hessian and substitute them into the second-order formula; verify the coefficients by multiplying the one-variable expansions.

items.title: A constrained extremum on an affine graph satisfies the graph Lagrange rule
items.strategy: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ on $y=x+1$ by completing the square in the graph parameter, then compute both gradients and the multiplier at the unique minimizer.

items.title: The degenerate constraint $x^2+y^2=0$ defeats the multiplier conclusion
items.strategy: The constraint set is the singleton origin, so $f(x,y)=x$ has a constrained extremum there. But $\nabla g(0,0)=0$ and $\nabla f(0,0)=(1,0)$, so no scalar multiplier can satisfy the usual equation.

Invertible Euclidean linear maps
Newton maps are uniform contractions near a point with invertible derivative
The Euclidean inverse function theorem
The Euclidean implicit function theorem with derivative formula

The real complex-squaring map is locally but not globally invertible off the origin
