items.title: A locally finite hat-function partition of unity on $\mathbb{R}$ subordinate to overlapping unit intervals
items.strategy: Write the piecewise-linear translates explicitly, verify only two are nonzero at each point, and compute their sum as one.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, a finite subordinate partition of unity for a two-set cover of a compact interval
items.strategy: Use one explicit cutoff function and its complement, then compare the construction with the compact Hausdorff existence theorem.

items.title: Point-finite need not mean locally finite: intervals accumulating at the origin
items.strategy: Give an explicit family in $\mathbb{R}$ whose every point lies in finitely many members but every neighbourhood of the origin meets infinitely many.

items.title: Without local finiteness, a pointwise finite sum of continuous functions can be discontinuous
items.strategy: Use narrow triangular bumps accumulating at the origin, with disjoint supports away from the origin and heights bounded away from zero.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, $\omega_1$ is countably compact, noncompact, and not paracompact
items.strategy: Combine the published ordinal compactness computation with countably compact plus paracompact Hausdorff implies compact.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, paracompactness is not open-hereditary: $\omega_1$ inside $\omega_1+1$
items.strategy: The successor ordinal is compact and hence paracompact, while its open initial segment is the preceding nonparacompact example.

items.title: Assuming choice, two paracompact lower-limit lines can have a nonparacompact product
items.strategy: Expand the locally reconstructed lower-limit witness from the A-page and isolate the failure of Lindelöfness in the antidiagonal.

pages.title: The Tychonoff Embedding and the Stone–Čech Compactification

items.title: A family of continuous unit-interval-valued functions that separates points from closed sets
The evaluation map from a space into the unit cube indexed by a family of continuous functions
The evaluation map of a point–closed-set separating family is a topological embedding
items.strategy: Prove continuity coordinatewise, injectivity by separating one point from the singleton containing the other, and recovery of the source topology by separating a point from the complement of an arbitrary neighbourhood.

items.title: A space is Tychonoff if and only if it embeds in a cube $[0,1]^J$
items.strategy: Use all continuous maps to the unit interval for the forward evaluation embedding. For the reverse implication use productivity and heredity of complete regularity and of the $T_1$ axiom.

items.title: A Hausdorff compactification as a dense embedding into a compact Hausdorff space
Assuming the ultrafilter lemma, every Tychonoff space has a Hausdorff compactification
items.strategy: Embed the space in its unit cube, use compactness of the cube under the ultrafilter lemma, and take the closure of the image.

items.title: The Stone–Čech compactification by its compact-Hausdorff extension property
Every continuous $[0,1]$-valued function extends uniquely over the closure of the full evaluation image
items.strategy: Use the function's coordinate projection for existence and uniqueness of continuous extensions from agreement on the dense evaluation image.

items.title: Under dependent choice, every compact Hausdorff space embeds in a unit cube
items.strategy: Apply the published compact-Hausdorff-to-Tychonoff result and then the Tychonoff embedding theorem, keeping dependent choice explicit.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma and dependent choice, the closure of the full evaluation image is the Stone–Čech compactification
items.strategy: Extend the coordinates of a map into a compact Hausdorff target's cube, assemble them into a continuous product map, and show its image lies in the closed embedded target because the dense image already does. Use density and Hausdorffness for uniqueness.

items.title: Stone–Čech compactifications are uniquely homeomorphic over the original space
items.strategy: Apply the two universal properties to obtain maps in both directions and use uniqueness on the dense copy to show that the composites are identities.

items.title: The Stone–Čech compactification of a compact Hausdorff space adds no points
items.strategy: The compact embedded image is closed in the Hausdorff compactification and is dense, hence equals the whole compactification.

pages.title: The Tychonoff Embedding and the Stone–Čech Compactification: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A finite discrete space is already its Stone–Čech compactification
items.strategy: Verify compactness and Hausdorffness directly and invoke the compact-Hausdorff fixed-point corollary.

items.title: Every function from discrete $\mathbb N$ to $[0,1]$ extends uniquely to $\beta\mathbb N$
items.strategy: Every map from a discrete domain is continuous, so the Stone–Čech extension property applies directly; uniqueness comes from density and Hausdorffness.

items.title: The one-point compactification of discrete $\mathbb N$ is not $\beta\mathbb N$
items.strategy: Use the parity-valued function on the discrete naturals. Any extension to the point at infinity would have to be eventually close to a single value, while both parity classes meet every cofinite neighbourhood.

items.title: FALSE: every Hausdorff compactification has the Stone–Čech extension property
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the one-point compactification of the discrete naturals and its nonextendable parity function.

pages.title: Countability Axioms and Cardinal Functions

items.title: Second countability: an at most countable basis for the topology
Separability: the existence of an at most countable dense subset
The countable chain condition: every pairwise-disjoint family of nonempty open sets is at most countable
Under choice, weight $w(X)$, density $d(X)$, local character $\chi(x,X)$, and character $\chi(X)$ as raw cardinal minima and a supremum
Under choice, Lindelöf degree $L(X)$ and cellularity $c(X)$ as raw cardinal functions
Under choice, $w(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: The topology itself is a basis, so the nonempty set of cardinalities of bases has a least member.

items.title: Under choice, $d(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: The whole space is dense in itself, so the cardinalities of dense subsets form a nonempty set of cardinals and have a least member.

items.title: Under choice, $\chi(x,X)$ and $\chi(X)$ are well-defined cardinals
items.strategy: The neighbourhood filter is a local base; take the least local-base cardinal at each point and the cardinal supremum over the resulting set.

items.title: Under choice, $L(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: Every open cover is a subfamily of the topology and is itself a subcover, so one cardinal bound works; take the least working cardinal.

items.title: Under choice, $c(X)$ is a well-defined cardinal
items.strategy: Every disjoint family of nonempty open sets is a subfamily of the topology, so its cardinality is bounded; take the supremum of the resulting set of cardinals.

items.title: Under choice, the five cardinal functions recover first countability, second countability, separability, Lindelöfness, and ccc at the $\aleph_0$ threshold
items.strategy: Unpack the five definitions, using the library's convention that countable means at most countable.

items.title: A countable local base can be chosen open and decreasing
items.strategy: Extract the construction already used in the published sequence theorem: enumerate the base, replace members by open neighbourhoods, and take running finite intersections.

items.title: Every second countable space is first countable
items.strategy: At a point retain the members of a global countable basis that contain it.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is separable
items.strategy: Choose one point from each nonempty member of a countable basis; the chosen set meets every nonempty basic open set.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is Lindelöf
items.strategy: For each basis member lying inside a member of the cover, choose one such cover member; the selected countable family covers.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a metrizable space is second countable if and only if it is separable if and only if it is Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use rational-radius balls around a countable dense set for separable implies second countable, the general second-countable implication, and countable subcovers of the radius-$1/n$ ball covers for Lindelöf implies separable.

items.title: Second countability is hereditary
items.strategy: Take traces of a countable ambient basis.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of second countable spaces is second countable
items.strategy: Choose a countable basis in each factor and enumerate the finite-support boxes using countable unions of finite products of countable sets.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of first countable spaces is first countable
items.strategy: At a point enumerate finite-support products of chosen countable local bases.

items.title: Every separable space satisfies the countable chain condition
items.strategy: Enumerate a countable dense set and assign to each disjoint nonempty open set the least enumerated point it contains; disjointness makes the assignment injective.

items.title: Under choice, $c(X)\le d(X)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(X),L(X)\le w(X)$
items.strategy: Choose a point from each nonempty basis element for density; assign a least dense point to each disjoint open set; obtain local bases by restriction and cover subfamilies by choosing one cover member above each eligible basis element.

items.title: Under choice, for $Y\subseteq X$, $w(Y)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(y,Y)\le\chi(y,X)$
items.strategy: Trace a basis and local bases to the subspace.

items.title: Under choice, a continuous surjection does not increase density or Lindelöf degree
items.strategy: The image of a dense set is dense under a surjection, and an open cover of the codomain pulls back to one of the domain.

items.title: Under choice, every metrizable space has $w(X)=d(X)$
items.strategy: The basic inequality gives $d\le w$; rational-radius balls around a least dense set give $w\le d$ for infinite density, while the finite case is discrete and checked separately.

items.title: Under choice, the uncountable $\Delta$-system lemma for finite sets
items.strategy: Thin to a fixed finite size, induct on that size, and use the uncountable pigeonhole split according to whether one point occurs uncountably often.

items.title: Under choice, every Cantor cube $2^I$ satisfies ccc
items.strategy: An uncountable family of basic cylinders has finite supports; thin the supports to a delta system and then thin again so the finitely many root coordinates carry one common pattern, forcing two cylinders to meet.

items.title: Under choice, if $|I|>2^{\aleph_0}$, then the Cantor cube $2^I$ is not separable
items.strategy: A countable set of points induces at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ coordinate columns; two equal columns leave a two-coordinate basic cylinder disjoint from the alleged dense set.

items.title: Assuming choice, refuted: every ccc space is separable
items.strategy: Take a Cantor cube indexed by a cardinal strictly above $2^{\aleph_0}$.

items.title: Refuted: every first countable space is second countable
items.strategy: Use an uncountable discrete space: singleton local bases give first countability, while every global basis must contain every singleton.

items.title: Refuted: every separable space is second countable
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit line locally, use the rationals for separability, and inject the reals into any basis by choosing a basis member whose left endpoint is forced at each point.

items.title: Refuted: separability is hereditary
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit plane locally: its rational grid is dense, while its uncountable discrete antidiagonal has no proper dense subset.

items.title: Refuted: Lindelöfness is hereditary
items.strategy: Take the one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space; the whole space is compact while the open discrete subspace is not Lindelöf.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, refuted: Lindelöfness is productive
items.strategy: Rebuild the lower-limit line: thin covers by rational intervals to prove it Lindelöf, then use the closed uncountable discrete antidiagonal to show its square is not.

items.title: Assuming choice and countable choice, refuted: arbitrary products of second countable spaces are second countable
items.strategy: A sufficiently large Cantor cube has second countable two-point factors but is not separable, whereas second countability would imply separability under countable choice.

items.title: Under choice, for the usual real line, $w=d=\chi=L=c=\aleph_0$ under the raw convention
items.strategy: Use rational intervals and rational points for the upper bounds, then rule out finite bases, dense sets, and local bases and exhibit arbitrarily large finite disjoint open families and covers.

items.title: Under choice, for an infinite discrete space of cardinality $\kappa$, $w=d=L=c=\kappa$ while $\chi=1$
items.strategy: Singletons force the basis, dense set, and cellular family; the singleton at a point is a one-member local base, and the singleton cover forces the Lindelöf degree.

items.title: For the lower-limit line, $\chi=d=L=c=\aleph_0$ and $w=2^{\aleph_0}$ under choice
items.strategy: Reconstruct the half-open basis, use rational density and the Lindelöf thinning argument, force distinct basis members at distinct left endpoints, and bound disjoint open families by density.

items.title: Assuming choice, the lower-limit plane is first countable, separable, and ccc, but not second countable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use product local bases and the rational grid, inherit ccc from separability, and use the uncountable closed discrete antidiagonal for the two failures.

items.title: The one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space is compact and Lindelöf but need not be first countable or separable
items.strategy: Neighbourhoods of infinity have finite complements; a countable local base would make the discrete part countable, and density must contain every isolated point.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, $\omega_1$ is first countable and countably compact but is not separable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Build countable cofinal local bases below each countable ordinal, then use boundedness of countable subsets and the standard initial-segment cover.

items.title: Under choice, a concrete ccc nonseparable Cantor cube indexed above $2^{\aleph_0}$
items.strategy: Take the index set to be a power set of a set of size $2^{\aleph_0}$ and apply the delta-system ccc theorem and repeated-column nonseparability lemma.

items.title: Assuming choice, a separable space with a nonseparable subspace: the lower-limit plane and its antidiagonal
items.strategy: Expand the rectangle calculation showing the rational grid is dense and every antidiagonal singleton is subspace-open.

items.title: Assuming choice, a Lindelöf space whose square is not Lindelöf: the lower-limit line
items.strategy: Expand the rational-endpoint cover thinning in the factor and the closed-discrete obstruction in the square.

items.title: Discrete families and $\sigma$-locally-finite and $\sigma$-discrete bases
Every discrete family is locally finite, so every $\sigma$-discrete basis is $\sigma$-locally finite
items.strategy: Unfold the two neighbourhood conditions and then retain the same countable decomposition.

items.title: A locally metrizable space: every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood
Compatible normal sequences of open covers
A $T_1$ space with a compatible normal sequence of open covers is metrizable
items.strategy: Construct dyadic-scale symmetric entourages from successive star refinements, define the chain infimum pseudometric, prove the triangle inequality, and use compatibility plus $T_1$ to obtain point separation and the original topology.

items.title: Under choice, every metric space has a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis
items.strategy: For each positive scale refine the cover by balls of that scale locally finitely using Stone's theorem; the union of these refinements is a basis because the mesh tends to zero.

items.title: Under choice, a regular $T_1$ space with a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis has a compatible normal sequence
items.strategy: Record the source-backed normal-cover construction as an explicitly external fallback after the local pointwise-shrinking route is shown invalid; retain no fictitious local dependency edge.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is regular, $T_1$, and has a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis
items.strategy: Use the metric-basis lemma for necessity. For sufficiency turn the basis into a compatible normal sequence and apply the Alexandroff–Urysohn metrization lemma.

items.title: Under choice, every metric space has a $\sigma$-discrete basis
items.strategy: Record Bing's source-backed necessity construction as an explicitly external fallback after the proposed first-centre cells are shown not to be open; retain no fictitious local dependency edge.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is regular, $T_1$, and has a $\sigma$-discrete basis
items.strategy: Use the sigma-discrete basis lemma for necessity. For sufficiency a discrete family is locally finite and Nagata–Smirnov applies.

items.title: Under choice, every regular $T_1$ second-countable space is metrizable
items.strategy: Enumerate a countable basis as a countable union of singleton, hence locally finite, families and apply Nagata–Smirnov.

items.title: A locally finite open cover by subspaces with $\sigma$-locally-finite bases yields a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis of the whole space
items.strategy: At each countable layer take the union of the corresponding relative bases. Local finiteness of the cover reduces the neighbourhood check to finitely many subspaces, and openness of the cover members makes the union a basis.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is paracompact, Hausdorff, and locally metrizable
items.strategy: For sufficiency refine the cover by metrizable neighbourhoods locally finitely, take sigma-locally-finite bases in the refinements, merge them, and apply Nagata–Smirnov using paracompact Hausdorff regularity. For necessity use Stone's theorem and the space itself as a metrizable neighbourhood.

items.title: An uncountable discrete space is metrizable and has a discrete basis, but is not second countable
items.strategy: Use the zero-one discrete metric and the singleton basis; any basis must contain every singleton, so an uncountable underlying set prevents second countability.

items.title: Under choice, the lower-limit line is regular and separable but not second countable and therefore not metrizable
items.strategy: Use the published clopen basis and rational density. A putative countable basis must assign to every real point a distinct basis member whose least point is that real; this contradicts uncountability. The metric countability equivalence then rules out metrizability.

items.title: FALSE: every regular space is metrizable
items.strategy: Use the regular nonmetrizable lower-limit line and identify its missing countability hypothesis.

items.title: Under choice, the Niemytzki plane is Tychonoff and locally metrizable but not normal, paracompact, or metrizable
items.strategy: Build the tangent-disk basis and verify its point-separation and local metrization directly. Prove complete regularity with explicit tangent-disk bump functions. Its countable dense upper-half-plane subset and uncountable closed discrete boundary contradict Jones's normal-space bound; Stone and paracompact-Hausdorff normality then rule out metrizability and paracompactness.

pages.title: Uniform Completeness, Completion, and the Samuel Compactification

items.title: The Samuel uniformity generated by bounded uniformly continuous functions
Samuel function pseudometrics generate a uniformity coarser than the original one
items.strategy: For each uniformly continuous f:X-> [0,1], verify that p_f(x,y)=|f(x)-f(y)| is a pseudometric by the real absolute-value laws. Pull every p_f-ball back from the metric uniformity of [0,1]; finite intersections then show that the generated Samuel uniformity is coarser than the original uniformity.

items.title: The Samuel uniformity is totally bounded
items.strategy: Fix a basic entourage involving finitely many [0,1]-valued coordinates. Choose a finite small net in [0,1] for each coordinate, partition X into the finitely many nonempty coordinate cells, and use finite choice to select one representative from each cell. Treat the empty coordinate family and the empty space separately.

items.title: Assuming dependent choice, the Samuel uniformity induces the original topology
items.strategy: Coarsening gives one topological inclusion. For an original neighbourhood O of x, choose U[x] inside O, build a normal entourage sequence and its controlled pseudometric p, and use f(y)=min(1,4p(x,y)). The Samuel f-ball of radius one at x lies in O. Include the empty space explicitly.

items.title: The Samuel completion and, when compactifying, the Samuel compactification
Total boundedness passes to a uniform space with a dense uniformly continuous image
items.strategy: Given a target entourage, choose a symmetric entourage whose square is smaller and pull it back by uniform continuity. Cover the source by finitely many pulled-back balls. Density supplies a source image point near each target point, and a two-entourage composition puts that target point near the image of one of the finite source centres. Separate the empty target case.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma the Samuel completion is compact, and under dependent choice plus the ultrafilter lemma it compactifies every separated uniform space
items.strategy: The Samuel uniformity is totally bounded, and the dense completion remains totally bounded. Completeness plus total boundedness gives compactness under the ultrafilter lemma. Under dependent choice the Samuel and original topologies agree; for a separated original uniformity this makes the completion map a topological embedding with dense image. With both choice principles it is therefore a compactification.

items.title: Under dependent choice and the ultrafilter lemma, uniformly continuous maps to compact Hausdorff spaces extend uniquely over the Samuel compactification
items.strategy: Give a compact Hausdorff target its unique compatible uniformity. Under dependent choice its topology is generated by the gauge of continuous [0,1]-valued functions. Composing those coordinate functions with the given uniformly continuous map shows that the map is uniformly continuous from the Samuel uniformity. Compactness makes the target complete, so the uniform-completion universal property gives the extension and density gives uniqueness.

items.title: Samuel compactifications are unique up to the unique isomorphism fixing the original space
items.strategy: Apply the compact-target extension property in both directions between two Samuel compactifications. The two composites agree with the identity on the dense original image, so uniqueness makes them identities.

items.title: Assuming dependent choice, a totally bounded uniformity equals its Samuel uniformity
items.strategy: For an original entourage U, construct a bounded controlled pseudometric p with a quarter-ball inside U. A finite p-net supplies finitely many distance functions f_z(y)=p(z,y). A sufficiently small simultaneous Samuel entourage for those functions forces p(x,y)<1/4 and hence lies in U. Combine this with the already proved coarsening and treat the empty space.

items.title: Under dependent choice the Samuel completion of a separated totally bounded space is its uniform completion; under the ultrafilter lemma it is compact
items.strategy: The preceding equality identifies the original and Samuel uniformities, so their Hausdorff completions are the same up to the unique uniform isomorphism fixing X. Under the ultrafilter lemma that completion is compact by completeness and total boundedness; keep this compactness clause separate from the DC identification.

items.title: Under dependent choice and the ultrafilter lemma, the Stone-Cech compactification maps continuously onto the Samuel compactification
items.strategy: A separated uniform space is Tychonoff under dependent choice, so use the evaluation-closure Stone-Cech compactification. Its universal property extends the Samuel compactification map. The image of the resulting map is compact and therefore closed in the Hausdorff Samuel compactification, while it contains the dense original image; hence it is onto.

pages.title: Uniform Completeness, Completion, and the Samuel Compactification: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The Samuel compactification of a compact Hausdorff space adds no points
items.strategy: Use the unique compatible uniformity. Compactness gives completeness and total boundedness, so the identity is already a Hausdorff completion; the totally bounded agreement theorem identifies it with the Samuel compactification. Include the empty compact space.

items.title: The Samuel compactification of the open unit interval is the closed unit interval
items.strategy: Give (0,1) and [0,1] their usual metric uniformities. For epsilon>0 choose n>=2 with 1/n<epsilon; the finite grid {j/n:1<=j<n} is an epsilon-net in (0,1), as the integer-part lemma supplies the adjacent grid index. The inclusion has dense image and exactly pulls back the closed interval's uniformity, and compact [0,1] is complete and separated. Thus [0,1] is its Hausdorff uniform completion, and the totally bounded agreement theorem identifies the Samuel compactification.

items.title: The Samuel compactification of the discrete natural numbers is beta N
items.strategy: Define the discrete metric on N directly and verify its metric axioms. Its radius-1/2 entourage is the diagonal, so every map from this discrete uniformity is uniformly continuous. Hence the Samuel extension property and the Stone-Cech extension property quantify over the same maps into compact Hausdorff targets. Apply the two uniqueness arguments to identify the compactifications over N.

items.title: The Samuel compactification map need not be a uniform embedding for the original uniformity
items.strategy: Use the infinite discrete natural numbers and verify the discrete metric directly. Its radius-1/2 entourage balls are singletons, so a finite such ball cover would make N finite, contradicting the pigeonhole theorem. Thus the original uniformity is not totally bounded, while the Samuel uniformity is totally bounded. The completion map pulls back precisely the Samuel uniformity, so it cannot also pull back the strictly finer original discrete uniformity. Distinguish this from its being a topological embedding under dependent choice.

items.title: The Samuel reflection of a nonempty indiscrete uniform space is a singleton
items.strategy: For the indiscrete uniformity {X x X}, uniform continuity into [0,1] forces every Samuel coordinate function to be constant. The generated Samuel uniformity is therefore indiscrete, its separated quotient identifies every pair of points, and its Hausdorff completion is the one-point space.

items.strategy: verify direct-image functoriality and the naturality equation on an arbitrary element

items.title: The opposite-group functor is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor by inversion
items.strategy: check inversion is a homomorphism into the opposite group and use preservation of inverses for naturality

items.title: The distributive and exponential laws of sets are natural isomorphisms
items.strategy: write the elementwise bijections and verify their inverse and naturality equations in every variable

items.title: For \(n\ge 1\), determinant is a natural transformation \(\det:\operatorname{GL}_n(-)\Rightarrow(-)^{\times}\) from commutative rings to groups
items.strategy: define both group-valued functors and verify the naturality square from the Leibniz formula

items.title: Actions of a group \(G\) on sets are functors \(BG\to\mathbf{Set}\)
An action groupoid has the acted-on set as objects, orbits as connected components, and stabilizers as automorphism groups
A path between basepoints induces an isomorphism of fundamental groups
A functor need not preserve monomorphisms
The injection \(\varnothing\to\{*\}\) is monic in \(\mathbf{Set}\) but is not split
A two-object indiscrete preorder is equivalent but not isomorphic to its one-object poset reflection
The inclusion of one object into a discrete two-object category is fully faithful but not essentially surjective
A componentwise family between functors need not be a natural transformation
Every equivalence of categories is an isomorphism of categories
Every morphism that is both monic and epic is an isomorphism
Every category is locally small
A natural transformation is determined by its component at one object

pages.title: Universal Properties, Representables and the Yoneda Lemma

items.title: The covariant and contravariant hom-assignments and the hom-bifunctor of a locally small category
The assignments $\mathcal C(a,-)$ and $\mathcal C(-,a)$ are functors to $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: For a morphism $u:b\to c$, define the covariant action by postcomposition $f\mapsto u\circ f$ and the contravariant action by precomposition $g\mapsto g\circ u$. Associativity gives preservation of composition, and the identity laws give preservation of identities.

items.title: The hom-assignment $\mathcal C(-,-):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a bifunctor
items.strategy: Send $(h:a'\to a,u:b\to b')$ to $f\mapsto u\circ f\circ h$. Check identity and composition componentwise; associativity also shows that precomposition and postcomposition commute, so the two one-variable hom-functors assemble into one bifunctor.

items.title: Generalized elements and their shapes
Presheaves, covariantly and contravariantly representable functors, and representations
Initial and terminal objects are exactly the representations of the constant singleton functor
items.strategy: For the covariant case, a representation $\mathcal C(I,-)\cong 1$ says that every hom-set out of $I$ is a singleton, exactly the initial-object condition. Apply the same argument to $\mathcal C(-,T)\cong1$ for terminal objects, including the empty-category obstruction.

items.title: Initial and terminal objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Between two initial objects there is one morphism in each direction. Each composite is an endomorphism of an initial object and hence must be its unique endomorphism, the identity; uniqueness of the isomorphism follows from uniqueness of the forward morphism. Dualize for terminal objects.

items.title: Evaluation at the identity gives $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ and proves that the natural-transformation collection is a set
items.strategy: Define evaluation by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_a(1_a)$. For $x\in F(a)$ construct $\alpha^x_c(f)=F(f)(x)$, check naturality, and prove the two constructions inverse using the naturality square for $f:a\to c$. Only after this explicit bijection is constructed identify the natural-transformation collection with a set; no choice is used.

items.title: The Yoneda bijection $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ is natural in both $a$ and $F$
items.strategy: Use the explicit evaluation bijection. For $h:a\to a'$, verify that precomposition with $\mathcal C(h,-):\mathcal C(a',-)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(a,-)$ corresponds to $F(h)$; for $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$, verify that postcomposition by $\eta$ corresponds to $\eta_a$. These two equations establish the two naturality squares without assuming a functor category for a large source.

items.title: For a presheaf $P$, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),P)\cong P(a)$ naturally in $a$ and $P$
items.strategy: Apply the covariant Yoneda lemma to $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$. Translate its covariant hom-functor, object morphisms, and naturality equations back to the stated presheaf variance.

items.title: Local smallness does not make every natural-transformation collection a set, but the Yoneda construction proves sethood in the representable-source case
The Yoneda assignment and the small-source Yoneda functor, traditionally called the Yoneda embedding
The Yoneda functor is fully faithful, and it is a full embedding when its object map is injective
items.strategy: Specialize contravariant Yoneda to $P=\mathcal C(-,b)$ to obtain $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),\mathcal C(-,b))\cong\mathcal C(a,b)$. Check that the inverse sends $f:a\to b$ to postcomposition by $f$, exactly the morphism action of $y$; the bijection gives fullness and faithfulness with no global smallness needed for the hom-set claim. Under the library's stronger terminology, add the conditional object-injectivity clause before calling this a full embedding.

items.title: Objects $a$ and $b$ are isomorphic exactly when $\mathcal C(-,a)$ and $\mathcal C(-,b)$ are naturally isomorphic
items.strategy: An isomorphism $a\to b$ is sent by Yoneda to a natural isomorphism. Conversely, full faithfulness lifts a natural isomorphism and its inverse to morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$; faithfulness turns the two inverse equations into the corresponding equations in $\mathcal C$.

items.title: Universal elements of covariant functors and presheaves
A representation is equivalently a universal element with a unique factorisation property
items.strategy: For covariant $F$, send a representation $\theta:\mathcal C(R,-)\cong F$ to $u=\theta_R(1_R)$ and use Yoneda's inverse formula to show $\theta_c(f)=F(f)(u)$. Conversely the stipulated unique factorization makes each such map bijective, and functoriality makes the family natural. Apply the dual argument to presheaves.

items.title: Representing objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with their universal elements
items.strategy: Given universal elements $(R,u)$ and $(R',u')$ for the same covariant functor, use universality to obtain the unique maps $i:R\to R'$ and $j:R'\to R$ carrying one universal element to the other. Functoriality and uniqueness force $ji=1_R$ and $ij=1_{R'}$, and also force uniqueness of the compatible isomorphism; dualize for presheaves.

items.title: The category of elements of a covariant functor or a presheaf
Universal elements are initial in a covariant category of elements and terminal in a presheaf category of elements
items.strategy: Unpack a morphism $(R,u)\to(c,x)$ in the covariant category of elements: it is exactly a morphism $f:R\to c$ satisfying $F(f)(u)=x$, so initiality is precisely the universal-factorization condition. The presheaf equation reverses the arrow and yields terminality.

items.title: Universal arrows from an object to a functor and from a functor to an object
Universal arrows to a functor are initial in comma categories, and universal arrows from a functor are terminal
items.strategy: An arrow in $(X\downarrow U)$ from $(R,\eta)$ to $(C,f)$ is a morphism $h:R\to C$ with $U(h)\eta=f$, exactly the unique factorization in a universal arrow from $X$ to $U$. Unpack $(U\downarrow X)$ dually for universal arrows from $U$ to $X$.

pages.title: Universal Properties, Representables and the Yoneda Lemma — Examples

items.title: A Cartesian product represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,A)\times\mathbf{Set}(X,B)$
items.strategy: Use $A\times B$ with its projections. Send $f:X\to A\times B$ to its two coordinate maps, send a pair $(g,h)$ to $x\mapsto(g(x),h(x))$, and check that these operations are inverse and natural in $X$.

items.title: A tagged disjoint union represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(A,X)\times\mathbf{Set}(B,X)$
items.strategy: Construct $A\sqcup B=(A\times\{0\})\cup(B\times\{1\})$. Restriction along the two injections sends a map out of the union to a pair of maps; define the inverse piecewise on the two tags and verify uniqueness and naturality.

items.title: The function set $B^A$ represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X\times A,B)$
items.strategy: Curry a map $f:X\times A\to B$ to $x\mapsto(a\mapsto f(x,a))$ and uncurry a map $X\to B^A$ by evaluation. The two formulas are inverse and commute with precomposition in $X$.

items.title: The free word monoid on $X$ represents $M\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(M))$
items.strategy: Form the monoid $X^*$ of finite words under concatenation and the one-letter map $j:X\to X^*$. Extend $f:X\to U(M)$ to the product of the letters in a word, prove this is the unique unital monoid homomorphism extending $f$, and check naturality in $M$. Also verify that monoids and unital homomorphisms form a locally small category and that $U$ is a functor.

items.title: The free group on $X$ represents $G\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$
items.strategy: Apply the published free-group universal property to obtain a bijection $\mathbf{Grp}(F(X),G)\cong\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$. Show that postcomposition by a group homomorphism agrees with postcomposition of the underlying set map, proving naturality; for a singleton $X$, identify $F(X)$ with the infinite cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb Z[x]$ represents the underlying-set functor on unital rings
items.strategy: For an arbitrary unital ring $R$ and $r\in R$, define evaluation by $\sum_i a_i x^i\mapsto\sum_i(a_i1_R)r^i$. Integer scalars are central, so the convolution calculation proves multiplicativity without assuming $R$ commutative. Show that every unital homomorphism $\mathbb Z[x]\to R$ is forced by the image of $x$, and verify naturality under postcomposition.

items.title: The one-point space represents the underlying-set functor on $\mathbf{Top}$
items.strategy: A map from the one-point space $1$ to $X$ is determined by its unique image point, and every such map is continuous because each preimage is either empty or all of $1$. This gives $\mathbf{Top}(1,X)\cong U(X)$, naturally under continuous maps.

items.title: A representable presheaf on a poset is the indicator of a principal down-set
items.strategy: View a poset $P$ as a category and fix $p\in P$. Compute $P(-,p)$ at $q$: it is a singleton when $q\le p$ and empty otherwise. The unique possible restriction maps display the presheaf completely and identify its nonempty support with the principal down-set of $p$.

items.title: The functor $D(X)=X\sqcup X$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ is not covariantly representable
items.strategy: Define $D$ on a function by applying it separately to the two tags. If $D\cong\mathbf{Set}(R,-)$, evaluation at a singleton would give a bijection from the two-element set $D(1)$ to the singleton $\mathbf{Set}(R,1)$, an immediate contradiction for every set $R$.

items.title: Two singleton sets give canonically isomorphic representations of the identity functor on $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: Represent the identity functor by $\{0\}$ and by $\{1\}$ through evaluation at the unique point. The unique bijection $\{0\}\to\{1\}$ is the unique isomorphism carrying one universal point to the other, illustrating compatibility rather than merely an arbitrary isomorphism.

items.title: The Yoneda embedding of the walking-arrow category computed objectwise
items.strategy: For the category $0\xrightarrow{u}1$, tabulate $y(0)$ and $y(1)$ on both objects and on $u^{\mathrm{op}}$, then compute $y(u):y(0)\Rightarrow y(1)$. The resulting natural-transformation sets reproduce the three hom-sets and their composition.

items.title: For a monoid action, Yoneda says that an equivariant map from the regular action is determined by the identity element
items.strategy: View a monoid $M$ as its one-object category and a functor $BM\to\mathbf{Set}$ as a left $M$-set $X$. Identify $BM(*,-)$ with the left regular action on $M$; evaluation at the identity sends an equivariant map $M\to X$ to a point of $X$, with inverse $x\mapsto(m\mapsto m\cdot x)$.

items.title: The Yoneda lemma requires its category to be small
items.strategy: Refute the claim by the proved theorem: its construction uses only that each $\mathcal C(a,c)$ is a set. The large locally small category $\mathbf{Set}$ supplies a concrete category outside the small case, while the same evaluation-and-inverse formulas still apply.

items.title: Non-isomorphic objects can have naturally isomorphic representable presheaves
items.strategy: A natural isomorphism $\mathcal C(-,a)\cong\mathcal C(-,b)$ lifts by full faithfulness to mutually inverse morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$. This contradicts non-isomorphism and directly refutes the claim.

$H$-free and $\mathcal F$-free graphs under the induced-subgraph convention

Minimal forbidden induced subgraphs and forbidden bases
Every hereditary graph class is determined by its unique minimal forbidden induced subgraphs
Every nonempty hereditary graph class contains the null graph
The complement of a graph class
$\overline{G[W]}=\overline G[W]$ for every vertex set $W$
Complementation preserves hereditary classes and complements their minimal forbidden bases
$G$ is $H$-free if and only if $\overline G$ is $\overline H$-free
Cliques, stable sets, the clique number $\omega(G)$ and stability number $\alpha(G)$
Complementation swaps cliques with stable sets, so $\omega(\overline G)=\alpha(G)$
Anticonnected graphs and anticonnected components
The anticonnected components of $G$ are exactly the connected components of $\overline G$
Every graph with at least two vertices is connected or anticonnected
Edges between disjoint vertex sets; complete, anticomplete, pure and mixed pairs
Purity is symmetric; complementation swaps complete and anticomplete pairs and preserves mixed pairs
Distinct connected components are anticomplete, and distinct anticonnected components are complete
